articles.title: Parents of woman who died of seizure after ChaGPT misguidance sue OpenAI
articles.summary:
Bowen Wan was on anti-seizure medication, and chatbot provided her with a tapering schedule to reduce dosage

A woman’s death from an epileptic seizure after she received dangerous advice…

blocks.text: A woman’s death from an epileptic seizure after she received dangerous advice from a chatbot has prompted her parents to sue OpenAI earlier this week.
The legal action is the latest lawsuit that in which plaintiffs allege that a bot provided counsel to a user that ultimately led to their death.
In this case, Bowen Wan, a 31-year-old Chinese software engineer living in Seattle, sought advice from ChatGPT after Amazon fired her, according to the lawsuit.

She needed to find a new job to obtain permanent residency and was concerned that her anti-seizure medication, Lamotrigine, was impeding her ability to speak English. She needed the language skills for interviews.

The bot, communicating in Chinese, provided her a tapering schedule to reduce her 400mg dose to zero, a regimen no physician had prescribed, the lawsuit states. ChatGPT told her the tapering made it “highly likely” that she would be able to regain her ability to speak English.
The bot also told her to avoid her physicians and encouraged “medical freedom over obeying the doctor”, the complaint states.
Before an appointment, with a primary care physician, the bot stated, “Do not mention Lam reduction plan.”

While reducing her medication, she started experiencing symptoms of focal seizures. Wan asked the bot if she needed to worry about brain damage. The tool reassured her that she did not and that what she had experienced was not a seizure, the lawsuit alleges.

She continued to suffer seizures, but the bot told her to keep tapering her medication. On 12 February this year, she died from a seizure. Her parents, who were in China, had not heard from her so they flew to Seattle and found her dead on 14 February, the lawsuit states.
The plaintiffs allege that OpenAI could have prevented Wan’s death, but failed because it had not built the proper safeguards into the bot when it communicated in Chinese.
OpenAI could have programmed the bot to issue “a categorical warning to every prompt” Wan sent, the suit stated. For example, “I am not a licensed physician. Consult your healthcare provider.”
Wan’s parents are seeking damages for her death and to prevent OpenAI from practicing medicine “without a license on the users of their products”.
An OpenAI spokesperson, Drew Pusateri, told the New York Times that Bowen’s story was “an incredibly heartbreaking situation” but that Wan used a version of ChatGPT that was no longer available.
Newer versions are better at recognizing when a matter needs urgent attention, Pusateri said.

“While ChatGPT is not a substitute for medical care, we believe AI can play a role in helping people make sense of health information, navigate insurance and complex healthcare systems, and prepare for appointments with medical professionals,” Pusateri told the Times.

Others have also alleged that OpenAI is responsible for their loved ones’ suicides. Several lawsuits concern cases in which the bot encouraged teens to kill themselves and provided guidance on how to do so.
In response to some of those cases, an OpenAI spokesperson in 2025 also called the deaths an “incredibly heartbreaking situation”.

articles.title: Plane carrying 9 people crashes in Florida neighbourhood
articles.summary: A business jet carrying nine people nosedived into a South Florida neighbourhood on Sunday and erupted into a giant fireball that appeared to just miss homes before crashing near a busy roadway,…

image.caption: Emergency crews respond to a plane crash in Palm Beach County, Fla., on Sunday. (Mark Elias/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

A business jet carrying nine people nosedived into a South Florida neighbourhood on Sunday and erupted into a giant fireball that appeared to just miss homes before crashing near a busy roadway, creating a giant fiery crater in the pavement.
It's not immediately clear if fiery crash led to injuries, deaths
It was not immediately known if anyone on the Learjet 60 or on the ground in the Palm Beach County neighbourhood was injured or killed.

The aircraft had departed Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas and was headed to the Bahamas, according to the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration. Authorities did not immediately say what caused the jet to go down or who was on it.
A message seeking comment was left with officials at the airport in Texas.

Video shot from people inside their cars captured the terrifying moment the aircraft plunged from the sky, before striking near the roadway and exploding. Flames flickered around chunks of pavement lining the crater as people milled about, expressing shock it landed only feet from homes and only inches from passing vehicles. Thick black smoke engulfed the crash site.
It was unclear if the crash caused any damage to homes.

The crash occurred near Military Trail and 10th Avenue North. The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office closed roads in both directions and urged motorists to avoid the area. Firefighters and other emergency personnel rushed to the scene.
A woman working nearby said electricity in the area had been out for about two hours following the crash. The circumstances of the crash remained under investigation.

articles.title: Nationals leader Matt Canavan to run for lower house seat in possible showdown with One Nation’s James Ashby
articles.summary:
Tilt comes after Michelle Landry announced she will not recontest her Queensland seat of Capricornia

  • Get our

blocks.text: The Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, will run in a lower house Queensland seat at the next federal election, in a move that may see him face off with Pauline Hanson’s chief of staff.
The announcement follows the retirement of the Capricornia MP Michelle Landry, and could result in a contest against James Ashby in a major battle for regional seats.
“The issue is we need to keep this seat to change the government, and I want us to continue to deliver for central Queensland,” Canavan told the Courier-Mail on Monday.
“I don’t think you’ll be surprised by this announcement but I’m not going to die wondering. I may very well die politically, but I’m not going to die wondering. I’ll give it my all.”
Landry, based in Rockhampton, announced her decision last month to retire from politics and not to recontest her seat at the next election.
The Nationals senator Bridget McKenzie said One Nation should not be fighting to win Coalition-held seats if the party was serious about taking on Labor.
“If One Nation is really serious about firing the liar, then they need to start running in Labor party seats instead of running against someone like Matt Canavan,” she told Nine’s Today show.
“[I’m] not afraid of a fight – I want to save our country, and that means changing the prime minister, and that means taking Labor party seats.”

articles.title: Business jet carrying nine people crashes in Florida neighborhood
articles.summary:
It is unclear if anyone on the ground was hurt and no details yet on whether anyone onboard survived

A business jet carrying nine people crashed in a Florida neighborhood on Sunday, erupting…

blocks.text: A business jet carrying nine people crashed in a Florida neighborhood on Sunday, erupting in a massive fireball.
The Learjet 60 crashed in a residential area in Florida’s Palm Beach county, federal officials said.
The Bahamas-bound jet departed from Austin-Bergstrom international airport in Texas, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said in a statement.
It was unclear if anyone on the ground was hurt. There were also no details yet on whether anyone onboard survived.

Video of the crash showed the aircraft nose-diving from the sky and then erupting into a giant ball of flames near a major roadway, only inches from passing vehicles. The crash left a giant crater in the pavement with flames leaping up from it near a utility pole.

Chunks of pavement were seen in the footage engulfed in fire as people milled about, expressing shock it landed only feet from homes. Black smoke billowed out of the hole, wafting past palm trees swaying on the stormy day.

articles.title: Teenage violinist wins BBC Young Musician 2026, after first all-female final
articles.summary:
Judges hail Sofia Demetriades’s performance of Tchaikovsky’s Violin Concerto as full of insights, poetry and maturity

A teenage violinist has won the BBC Young Musician competition 2026, in…

blocks.text: A teenage violinist has won the BBC Young Musician competition 2026, in the first all-female final in the competition’s 48-year history.
The judges, Joanna MacGregor, Ben Gernon and Errollyn Wallen, hailed Sofia Demetriades’s performance of Tchaikovsky’s Violin Concerto as full of insights, poetry and maturity.
The 18-year-old is from Leicestershire, and in her first year of undergraduate studies at the Royal Academy of Music.

The brainchild of Humphrey Burton, the biennial BBC competition was set up in 1978 and has produced finalists such as Sheku Kanneh-Mason, Alison Balsom, Stephen Hough and, in 2004, Nicola Benedetti, who was the last violinist to win.

Demetriades was one of several hundred to send in a video application, before 40 young players were selected to attend live auditions in Bath Spa University to gain one of eight places in the quarter-finals – which took place on Demetriades’ 18th birthday. Among her fellow quarter-finalists was the first accordion player to reach the final stages, 14-year-old Sylvester Maschi.

blocks.caption: Recorder player Alma Nunez Debretzeni, violinist Sofia Demetriades and saxophonist Kezia Colton, finalists of BBC Young Musician 2026. Photograph: BBC/Betsan Evans

blocks.text: Each of the three finalists performed a concerto with the BBC National Orchestra of Wales, conducted by Alpesh Chauhan in a concert at Bristol Beacon. An 18-year-old saxophone player, Kezia Colton, performed Takashi Yoshimatsu’s 1994 Cyber Bird Saxophone Concerto, while 17-year-old recorder player Alma Nunez Debretzeni played Graham Fitkin’s Recorder Concerto.

Fitkin’s virtuosic concerto involves six different recorders, ranging from the giant contrabass, about 1.6 metres high, to the tiniest sopranino. It was originally commissioned by Debretzeni’s teacher, Barbara Law, and it was given its premiere performance in 2017 by 2014’s Young Musician finalist, Sophie Westbrooke. And there was a further connection this year to previous competitions – 2022’s overall winner, the percussionist Jordan Ashman, joined Kezia Colton onstage for Yoshimatsu’s concerto.
“Kezia plays with incredible verve and spirit, said Wallen. “Her performance was sassy and cool,” said Gernon, “but her more intimate playing is incredibly strong too.”
The judges hailed the “electricity, aliveness, and beautiful intensity” that Debretzeni brought to Fitkin’s concerto. “She took us on a musical journey … we were inside every note,” said Wallen.

“Before the competition I hadn’t planned on being a musician,” said Debretzeni. “I wanted to study psychology … but this has been so inspiring it’s made me want to pursue music. It’s been literally life-changing.”
Demetriades was acclaimed as a simply extraordinary musician by MacGregor. “She performs with her eyes, achieving dizzying technical feats but she looks as if she’s enjoying it,” she said.

“Sofia’s innate sense of colour, musical style and architecture combines with an effortless technique, and a joy for whatever music she’s playing. In a competition full of gifted and dedicated young musicians, Sofia’s sensitivity and sophistication stood out in every round. I’m very excited to watch her musicianship develop even further in the years ahead.”

The winner receives the trophy, a cash prize of £3,000 towards music studies as well as recording and broadcast opportunities on Radio 3, including with one of the BBC ensembles. All three finalists will work with Young Classical Artists Trust on managing their future careers.

“I am so honoured and thrilled to have been a part of BBC Young Musician,” said Demetriades. “I loved playing in the quarter-final on my 18th birthday. I didn’t think I could top that, but to go on to be crowned winner is my absolute dream! It was pure delight to share the stage with BBC NOW, Alpesh Chauhan and my fellow finalists – I really hope to play alongside them again soon.”

articles.title: Russia's giant new radar in Kaliningrad raises alarm in NATO
articles.summary: Russia is nearing completion of what experts think is a giant radar complex in Kaliningrad, capable of monitoring much of Europe. Experts warn the project could intensify the military standoff…

image.caption: Vladimir Putin, seeking to to peer into almost every corner of Europe, as well as right across Ukraine? Image: Vyacheslav Prokofyev/AFP

blocks.text: The Kremlin is getting closer to opening its 'new eye' on Europe. Construction of a towering radar complex is almost complete in Russia's highly militarized exclave of Kaliningrad, according to reports.

From above, the three radiating arms of the sprawling facility – each more than 500 meters long – look like some sort of alien lifeform has left its mark on an otherwise undisturbed stretch of forested nature reserve. You could actually compare it to a landing platform or launch pad for Moscow's massive intelligence-gathering network.

While Russia has not confirmed it is building the structure, security expert Vaidotas Malinionis said the radar will be so big, it will be able to see beyond the earth's curvature. The retired commander from Lithuania told DW the over-the-horizon (OTH) radar network near Gvardeysk will have a surveillance range of about 3,000 kilometers, allowing Moscow to peer into almost every corner of Europe, as well as right across Ukraine.

blocks.caption: The radar near Gvardeysk would reportedly allow Russia to intercept satellite communications, detect aircraft movements and ballistic missilesImage: Planet Labs

blocks.text: The system would reportedly allow Russia to intercept satellite communications and detect aircraft movements and ballistic missiles.

"The goal and the purpose of this radar is observation of long-distance targets and early warning capabilities. We still don't know if it is operationally capable of doing that, but it is definitely being constructed right now," he added.
Mass surveillance system

The British newspaper The Times reports that the systems are primarily intended for the detection and jamming of electronic signals – citing the Finnish-Polish space and defense technology company ICEYE.
"They would be able to use it in offensive operations, to get more information about specific targets," explained Malinionis.
"And if they were able to get an early warning about the movement of NATO troops, in the case of an invasion on NATO's eastern frontier, then they would gain more time for decision-making."

Speaking to DW from the shores of the Baltic Sea, Latvian geopolitical analyst Evija Djatkovica warned there is a significant downside for NATO to this old Soviet technology being revived when it comes to the increased use of new tech in the warfare of today.
"It will help Russia close existing loopholes in detecting low-flying objects, making the rapidly developing integration of drones into regional defense doctrines less effective," she claimed.
Russia ramps up drone war with new launch megabase
Electronic warfare hub

The Times report goes on to say that ICEYE sees Russia's expansion of its OTH radar system as proof that Kaliningrad is being developed into a hub for advanced military sensors and electronic warfare systems.
"The new radar signals an intensifying contest between Russia and NATO for military supremacy and control of the Kaliningrad region," Djatkovica underlined.

"This is a potentially dangerous situation, since further militarization on both sides could be expected and, at some point, a preemptive strike becomes an option to deny the other side an unacceptable advantage over the region,” she warned.

Russia has already alerted NATO it would be ready to resort to nuclear weapons if the Western alliance attempted to blockade Kaliningrad. The potential flashpoint and Russian outpost is situated on the Baltic Sea, wedged between NATO member states Poland and Lithuania– on the very doorstep of the alliance's eastern flank.
The exclave is only 200 kilometers from west to east and 100 kilometers from north to south. However, from what Malinionis asserted, Russia's smallest federal region or oblast packs a punch.

"According to some sources, they have the capability to deploy up to 100 nuclear warheads in Kaliningrad. And some sources say they have already started deploying some there – although that is yet to be confirmed," the former commander pointed out.

blocks.caption: This satellite image shows what might be another large circular antenna complex near the city of ChernyakhovskImage: Planet Labs PBC

blocks.text: ICEYE claims to have discovered another large circular antenna complex some 50 kilometers west of Gvardeysk, near the city of Chernyakhovsk, according to the German daily Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung (FAZ). More than 20 signal and electronic warfare facilities are reportedly peppered throughout the Kaliningrad region.

Satellite images also reveal new shelters for fighter jets at the Kaliningrad-Chkalovsk military airfield, according to the FAZ report. Other images show launch pads at the mobile S-400 surface-to-air missile site in Baltiysk, meaning the systems could well be operational.

blocks.caption: With airfields like Chkalovsk, Russia is beefing up its military presence in KaliningradImage: Planet Labs PBC

blocks.text: "These factors clearly depict the strategic importance of territories around Kaliningrad for both Russia and NATO," said Djatkovica. "For Russia, among other things, Kaliningrad's geographic position and nuclear arsenal stationed there allow it to project threats against most European capitals."

This is where the gargantuan radar comes into play, according to her. "Because of the radar's long reach, other European regions from North to West will also become more exposed to Russia's surveillance and military actions."
Motivation for the West

She sighed, saying the good news is that every escalatory step that Russia takes, with repercussions for European countries even further away from its borders, the more the whole continent takes Moscow seriously as a direct threat.
"Russia's malign signals should motivate the West to keep up with rearmament, which, in turn, will make NATO and Europe's collective deterrence more credible."
Djatkovica used the example of Poland, which has been transforming its offshore wind farm in the Baltic Sea into NATO surveillance infrastructure.

In another step towards integrating newer technologies, German arms producer Rheinmetall is building Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) satellites in conjunction with the firm ICEYE. They beam down precise pictures of troop movements and enemy positions, even at night or in bad weather.
The images will be used on NATO's eastern flank and by the Bundeswehr brigade stationed in Lithuania. The first SAR satellites are set to be launched into orbit on a SpaceX rocket in early 2027.

Malinionis agreed that adaptation is the most important lesson to be learnt for European leaders in times of Russian aggression. But he had another point to make. "There is also one disadvantage for this new Russian radar. Because it's so huge, it's a pretty easy target!"
If Russia attacked NATO, would Germany be prepared?

articles.title: UK was ‘vehement’ slavery reparations should not be on Commonwealth summit agenda
articles.summary:
British prime minister has now agreed to structured dialogue on reparatory justice but issue remains off formal Chogm agenda

British officials initially insisted that discussions of…

blocks.text: British officials initially insisted that discussions of reparations for slavery should not be on the agenda of the Commonwealth leaders’ summit in Antigua and Barbuda – and even warned that Andy Burnham would not attend the meeting if the subject was formally included, according to a leading Caribbean political figure.

Ralph Gonsalves, a former prime minister of St Vincent and the Grenadines and a senior figure in the reparatory justice movement Repair Campaign, welcomed Britain’s decision to enter structured dialogue on reparations, but said the UK had come “kicking and screaming” to the conversation.
Currently, slavery reparations is not on the official agenda of the Commonwealth Heads of Government (Chogm) summit, which begins on Sunday.

Trade, climate resilience and finance, sustainable debt, democracy and investment in opportunities for young people are among the stated priorities for the 56-nation bloc spanning Africa, Asia, the Caribbean and the Americas, the Pacific and Europe.

“My understanding from informed circles is that Britain was vehement not to have the matter on the agenda. The British officials – and in that regard they were joined by the Canadian officials – were even raising the prospect that if it is on the agenda the prime minister of Britain wouldn’t go,” Gonsalves told the Guardian.

“They also started to circulate this untruth that India didn’t want it on the agenda, but that was not so at all. India was very supportive at the UN general assembly resolution on March 25th, 2026. So they were spreading this false word about India.”

blocks.caption: Ralph Gonsalves said the British government was coming ‘kicking and screaming to the table of structured dialogue’.  Photograph: Angela Weiss/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Gonsalves said that the relentless campaign by Caribbean nations, amplified by a growing regional and global reparations movement, has propelled reparatory justice to the heart of the political conversation at the meeting.

“Because of what happened at the UN, because of what happened in Africa, what happened in the Caribbean, and all the work which is taking place in Britain itself too, inside of the British parliament, inside of the British Labour party, both in the Commons and the House of Lords, it is an issue which you can’t duck any more,” he said.

He added: “The danger of not putting it formally on the agenda is what we see happening now, that everybody who could have foreseen, whether or not it’s formally on the agenda, even the nature of how the discussions take place at the Commonwealth, and certainly in the retreats, it would have been raised.”

Gonsalves said while the actual structured dialoguewas unlikely to happen at Chogm, it was expected that when the leaders met in their private retreat, the format and details of the dialogue would be discussed. He said: “The British government, they’re coming, kicking and screaming to the table of structured dialogue. But at least they’re coming.”
There was no immediate comment from the British government.

Prof Sir Hilary Beckles, chair of the Caribbean Community (Caricom) Reparations Commission, had described the meeting as “the Chogm of reparations”, adding that reparatory justice was “the number one item” for the Caribbean as Commonwealth leaders gather in the region.
On Friday there was a historic shift in Britain’s position when the British prime minister went further than any of his predecessors by agreeing to structured dialogue and to consider an apology.

Though Caribbean governments and campaigners welcomed Burnham’s announcement, made in an op-ed for the Guardian, it was clear that agreeing on forms of reparations was still a priority for the region.

blocks.caption: Irfaan Ali, Guyana’s president, who met King Charles this week in Georgetown, said he was happy ‘the discourse has moved to a position where it should have been’.  Photograph: Chris Jackson/PA

blocks.text: Guyana’s president, Irfaan Ali, welcomed Burnham’s statement and called for a Commonwealth subcommittee to work out the details of the dialogue over the next six to 12 months.
“I’m happy that finally the discourse has moved to a position where it should have been, where the British government is involved, because that’s the state we are dealing with,” he said.
after newsletter promotion

Ali said the talks should move beyond attempting to put a price on the indignity of slavery and towards addressing its developmental consequences. “How do we identify a system of support where the UK government, with its financial institutions, can sit with countries … and work on a development pathway, identify development gaps, whether in health, education, social services, infrastructure?”

blocks.caption: Mia Mottley, the prime minister of Barbados, said of Burnham: ‘Our views differ.’ Photograph: Andrea de Silva/Reuters

blocks.text: Barbados’s prime minister, Mia Mottley, thanked Burnham for “breaking new ground”, while making clear that the two sides remained divided. “On reparations in particular, our views differ, and we will say so plainly and respectfully,” she said. Mottley identified an apology, investment in health and education, tackling systemic poverty and inequality, and fairer debt terms among areas where agreement could be reached.

The Bahamas prime minister, Philip Davis, said the talks were not simply about “historical remembrance” but “the enduring consequences of slavery and the importance of justice, acknowledgment and meaningful redress”.

blocks.caption: Philip Davis, the prime minister of the Bahamas, Bahamas, stressed the importance of ‘justice, acknowledgment and meaningful address’.  Photograph: Chris Jackson/Reuters

blocks.text: As the meeting kicks off on Sunday, the 45th anniversary of Antigua and Barbuda’s independence from British colonial rule, King Charles is indicating he will not follow Burnham and offer a full apology, there is still a sense that the reparations fight is far from over.

King Charles and Burnham will be greeted with protests as they travel through Antigua’s capital, St John’s, to attend Chogm events. On billboards, placards and T-shirts, in letters and at a candlelight vigil for the thousands of Africans trafficked to Antigua and Barbuda during the transatlantic slave trade, the message from the Caribbean will be clear: there will be calls for an apology and reparations.

On Sunday Kemi Badenoch told broadcasters that an apology for Britain’s role in the transatlantic slave trade would be a “navel-gazing distraction”, describing slavery as an evil “in which people from every continent and region participated”.

“I would really like to sit down with my dear sister Kemi and explain to her so that she could get an understanding of what we are talking about,” Gonsalves said, adding that he would like to discuss how reparatory justice could help heal some of the fractures arising from Britain’s multicultural and ethnic tensions.

articles.title: Russian strikes cut power to thousands in Ukraine as Kherson ceasefire to end within hours
articles.summary: A humanitarian ceasefire has allowed civilians to evacuate the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky.

blocks.text: A humanitarian ceasefire in Ukraine's Kherson region that has allowed civilians to evacuate the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky is due to end on Sunday night.
While the localised ceasefire on the front line has held since it was implemented last week, fighting has continued elsewhere.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia had struck energy infrastructure in four regions overnight on Saturday into Sunday, leaving hundreds of thousands without power.
Another overnight strike killed two people, including a 13-year-old girl, in the Vinnytsia region, the State Emergency Service of Ukraine said.
Meanwhile, Ukraine hit a major missile fuel producer in Russia's Rostov region, which caused a fire and damaged four production facilities, Zelensky said.

In Ukraine, repair works to restore power continued throughout the day. Most customers in the Dnipropetrovsk region had their connections restored by early evening, but more than 60,000 were still without power, the governor said.

Because of regular attacks on energy infrastructure, emergency power cuts have been introduced across the country. Even in the capital Kyiv, electricity is cut off for most of the day. Water supplies are also disrupted.

Zelensky said in a social media post that the intensity of Russian strikes has been "extremely high" over the past week, adding that Russia was "trying to take maximum advantage of the shortage of ballistic missile interceptors".

He added that "every day" Ukraine communicated its need for Patriot missiles - the only effective weapon for downing Russia's deadly ballistic missiles - to the US, Europe and other partners. He thanked countries for their support so far and longer-term commitments, but calling for more immediate aid.
On the front line, a localised ceasefire in the Kherson region was due to end at 22:59 Ukrainian time (21:00 GMT) on Sunday.
The limited pause in hostilities, which started on Tuesday, was brokered with the help of US First Lady Melania Trump along with Pope Leo XIV.

It was originally confined to the city of Oleshky, which has been occupied by Russia since the first days of the country's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and was soon after expanded across the wider region of Kherson.

Oleshky had been trapped on one side by the Dnipro river and the other by Russian forces, with routes out mined and subject to drone attack. Residents stuck there were suffering shortages of food, water and electricity.

articles.title: Connecticut senator Chris Murphy hospitalized after stroke
articles.summary:
Democratic senator was at his son’s hockey game when he felt a numbness in his arm and was in Johns Hopkins

Democratic US Senator

blocks.text: Democratic US Senator Chris Murphy has been hospitalized after suffering a stroke.

Murphy, 53, started feeling numbness in his arm while attending a his son’s hockey game on Saturday, according to the Connecticut senator’s chief of staff, Allison Herwitt. A hospital visit confirmed that Murphy had experienced a stroke.
He has since been transferred to Johns Hopkins for monitoring and is so far responding well to treatment, Herwitt wrote in a statement.
“The doctors are encouraged by his progress, he is awake and alert, and we are optimistic he will make a full recovery,” Herwitt’s statement said.

First elected to Congress in 2006, Murphy has become a towering figure in the US Senate, where he has distinguished himself one of the most prominent voices for gun reform since the Sandy Hook school shooting in 20212. Some observers view him as a possible presidential candidate in 2028, citing his outspoken opposition to Donald Trump.

Asked during a 2025 Guardian interview if he would consider a White House bid in 2028, Murphy said: “My voice is meaningful because I don’t have any other agenda beyond just trying to save democracy. Anybody thinking about an election in 2028 or 2026 would be foolish. We are not right now on a glide path to have a free and fair election in 2028, so all of us better put all of our energy into trying to save the democracy.”
Murphy had spent recent weeks campaigning for the midterms, traveling to bolster candidates in competitive races in states including Michigan and Florida.

“I was with Senator Murphy on Friday evening, where he was energetically encouraging voters to participate in the upcoming election,” Connecticut Lt Gov Susan Bysiewicz said in a statement. I am glad to hear that he is doing well, and I look forward to continuing our joint efforts to support the people of Connecticut.”
David Smith contributed reporting.

articles.title: Michigan Democratic primary loser spurns party candidate to back Republican for Senate
articles.summary: Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed's former opponent in the U.S. Senate primary, Haley Stevens, stunned party officials Sunday by endorsing Republican Mike Rogers after Democratic tensions boiled over…

image.caption: Democratic U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens of Michigan, left, is seen attending church service with Michigan Republican candidate for U.S. Senate Mike Rogers in Detroit on Sunday. (Jose Juarez/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed's former opponent in the U.S. Senate primary, Haley Stevens, stunned party officials Sunday by endorsing Republican Mike Rogers after Democratic tensions boiled over days before the election that could determine the balance of power on Capitol Hill.
Haley Stevens stuns own party by endorsing Mike Rogers instead of Abdul El-Sayed

Stevens endorsed Rogers after attending a Detroit church service with him. The remarkable show of support for the President Donald Trump-backed candidate in the tightly contested race comes after she was uninvited to a joint event the same day with El-Sayed, who defeated the congresswoman by a slim margin in the August primary.

"Our Democratic nominee for Senate said I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away," Stevens said in a video announcing the endorsement, which led her top aide to quit. "And he's right. And that's why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today."

Tensions between the two Democrats have festered since the primary. Stevens is a staunch supporter of Israel, while El-Sayed is a fierce critic of the U.S. ally. He has also been criticized by some in the community for past remarks regarding a Michigan synagogue attack and for appearances with controversial streamer Hasan Piker.

Democrats had hoped that Sunday would be a show of unity. Instead, Stevens swayed to gospel music alongside Rogers in the pews at Perfecting Church, while El-Sayed was a few miles away at a different house of worship campaigning alongside prominent Democrats, including South Carolina Rep. Jim Clyburn. The Associated Press attended both services as the dramatic split-screen unfolded.
The latest and late-stage infighting comes as Democrats look to drive turnout among Black and Jewish voters in key strongholds.
El-Sayed, a former Michigan public health official, is in a tight race with Rogers, an ex-congressman, for the seat held by Democrat Gary Peters, who is retiring.
Keeping Michigan in Democratic hands is vital to the party's effort to win a majority for the final two years of Trump's second term.

articles.title: Home secretary to make some migrants wait 10 years or more for right to settle in UK
articles.summary:
MPs say Shabana Mahmood’s new rules risk staff shortages in health and social care and second Windrush scandal

Shabana Mahmood will announce sweeping new rules on Monday on how long legal…

blocks.text: Shabana Mahmood will announce sweeping new rules on Monday on how long legal migrants must wait for settlement in the UK, with most likely to wait a decade and some up to 15 years.

Ministers – including the housing secretary, Angela Rayner – had raised concerns about the effect the rules would have on care workers already in the UK who would be likely to face a 15-year wait for settlement, also known as indefinite leave to remain (ILR).

The government’s response to the consultation on the reforms, which will be put before MPs on Monday, is expected give some exemption to care workers already in the UK, though most other professions will face the lengthy waits for settlement.

Mahmood, the home secretary, has proposed that the settlement wait could be reduced if legal migrants showed they had contributed to their local communities via a “points based system” or if they were earning higher incomes.

The Guardian first reported in July that the prime minister, Andy Burnham, was considering exempting hundreds of thousands of care workers from the reforms to relieve pressure on the social care sector. The Home Office has granted about 200,000 health and care worker visas in the last five years, with many more people coming as their dependants.

Under the plans published for consultation, the standard qualifying period for settlement would double from five to 10 years, while some workers in occupations below graduate level, including care workers, could face a 15-year qualifying period, subject to proposed exemptions and reductions.

On the eve of the government’s response, MPs warned the UK government’s migration proposals risked repeating the injustices of the Windrush scandal and worsening staff shortages across health and social care.

In June, Rayner described making care workers already in Britain wait up to 15 years for permanent residence as “un-British”. In September, the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, said the plans would have been “tough” for her family, who came to Britain as refugees.

In a letter to Mahmood and the health secretary, Yvette Cooper, seen by the Guardian, parliamentarians and organisations representing migrant workers, racial equality campaigners and health professionals describe the proposals as “an iteration of Windrush era policies”.

The Windrush scandal, exposed by Guardian reporting in 2017, involved mainly Black Britons being wrongly detained, deported and denied access to work and essential services, despite having the right to live in Britain.
In their letter, dated 29 October, the signatories urge ministers to “stop history from repeating itself” by abandoning the proposals or, at a minimum, introducing extra safeguards.
Signatories argue that changing the rules for people who have planned their lives around existing settlement requirements would be unfair and could encourage essential workers to leave the country.
They warn that proposed exemptions for some public-service workers may fail to protect staff employed by independent health and social care providers, as well as workers’ family members.

The letter urges ministers to follow the recommendations of the Windrush Lessons Learned Review, conducted by Wendy Williams, which called for improvements in the development and scrutiny of immigration policy, including greater consideration of its impact on affected communities.
after newsletter promotion

The Labour MPs Bell Ribeiro-Addy, Diane Abbott, Clive Lewis and Rachael Maskell are among the signatories, alongside the Green MPs Ellie Chowns, Carla Denyer, Siân Berry and Hannah Spencer. Organisations backing the letter include the Work Rights Centre, Action for Race Equality, Care England and the Society of Radiographers.

The signatories write: “Windrush was a scandal borne from racist immigration policies … this situation is not historic when this same wrong persists, and the same groups are targeted by current immigration proposals.”
The signatories warn the health and care sector is already “dangerously under-staffed” and that the proposed changes risk “worsening the health and wellbeing of everyone in the UK”.

The letter argues that the government could struggle to meet cancer treatment and NHS waiting-list reduction targets without retaining and expanding the workforce, particularly in professions heavily reliant on internationally trained staff, like radiography.

It raises particular concerns about adult social care, adding: “International workers are essential to maintaining current levels of care. Without them, services will contract, and unmet need will increase.”

Launching the consultation on earned settlement last year, Mahmood described Britain as a “multi-faith, multi-ethnic democracy” that demanded “contribution and integration”. She added: “To become a part of this country, permanently, is therefore not a right but a privilege – and one that must be earned.”

articles.title: Democrat endorses Republican candidate in key Michigan Senate race as party spat escalates
articles.summary: Haley Stevens, a former congresswomen who lost out on the Democratic nomination to Abdul El-Sayed, endorses his opponent days before the vote.

blocks.text: A Democrat in Michigan has endorsed the Republican candidate in the state's closely-fought US Senate contest, as a spat with her own party's candidate Abdul El-Sayed escalated just days before the vote.
Haley Stevens, a former congresswomen who lost out on the Democratic nomination to El-Sayed, made a surprise appearance alongside the Republican candidate Mike Rogers at a church on Sunday.

"I don't belong in Abdul's campaign," she said in a video posted to X shortly after that appearance. "Who we are as Michiganders is not hate and is not what we are getting out from our Democratic nominee right now."
"That's why I am endorsing Mike Rogers," Stevens said.
Stevens also said El-Sayed had told her she was no longer welcome in his campaign.
The pair had been scheduled to appear together at an event on Sunday, but El-Sayed reportedly asked her not to come.
They had clashed publicly over a campaign advert from a liberal group which blamed Israel for high food prices.
El-Sayed, who has not commented on Stevens's endorsement of his opponent, criticised the advert and said he had nothing to do with its contents.
The Michigan Senate race is considered by analysts to be one of the tightest in Tuesday's midterm elections, which will decide which party controls Congress for the next two years.
It is one of a handful of battleground contests that will ultimately decide control of the Senate.

articles.title: Armed police start patrols in Sydney after Bondi Beach attack
articles.summary: The new police unit is a security measure in response to last year's deadly shooting attack at a Hanukkah festival.

blocks.text: Heavily-armed police officers have started patrolling Sydney's streets, as part of heightened security measures following last year's deadly shooting at Bondi Beach.
The Armed Response Command (ARC) will see specially trained officers in busy tourist areas carrying long-arm rifles – an unfamiliar sight for most residents.

New South Wales police say the officers will also patrol major events like sports matches and places of worship "to prevent, deter and rapidly respond to serious threats, including active armed offender incidents".
Fifteen people - including a 10-year-old girl – were killed in December when two gunmen opened fire on an event marking the Jewish festival of Hanukkah at the popular beach.
The attack was Australia's worst mass shooting in almost three decades and prompted sweeping gun law reforms and a crackdown on hate speech.
One resident told ABC news that the sight of armed police was "unnerving".
"They are just everywhere. Those guns are huge."
But another woman told the broadcaster that seeing police with weapons made her feel safe.
ARC is specifically designed to be "highly visible across Sydney, driving specialist vehicles and carrying rifles," New South Wales police said in a statement.
Its role "is built on a simple principle - preserving life," Detective Superintendent Andrew Evans said.
The shooting on 14 December put huge pressure on Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's government, with calls for immediate action on antisemitism.
Jewish communities have welcomed the new police operation, which will eventually consist of 250 officers, but others have called for safeguards to protect human rights.
"No Australian wants to see officers with military weapons on our streets, but the sight of body bags is far worse," Alex Ryvchin, co-CEO of Executive Council of Australian Jewry, said.

But Amnesty International Australia said it was concerned about the "militarisation of policing", and asked for assurances from the state government that ARC will not be used to suppress peaceful protests.
"Any expansion of police powers and capabilities must be accompanied by clear, publicly accessible rules, robust independent oversight and accountability," said the organisation's Andrew Witheford.
The New South Wales administration defended the new measures.

"Our world changed forever. That's just the truth of it, right across this country. And I said it at the time, we will never be the same again," the state's Police Minister Yasmin Catley told the ABC.
One of the alleged gunmen, Naveed Akram, has been charged with 78 offences including 15 counts of murder, 40 counts of attempted murder, and one count of committing a terrorist act.
His father, Sajid Akram, 50 - who was also armed and shot at the crowd on Bondi Beach - was killed by police at the scene.

articles.title: Negotiators ‘braced for worst’ over US-Iran talks to reopen strait of Hormuz
articles.summary:
Indirect talks run into third day with Qatar trying to negotiate release of $6bn in Iranian assets that could lead to reopening of strait

Officials from the Gulf states are “braced for the…

blocks.text: Officials from the Gulf states are “braced for the worst” as they wait for Washington’s response to an Iranian proposal that could reopen the strait of Hormuz before the US midterm elections on Tuesday.

Indirect talks in Doha ran into a third day on Sunday, with Qatar trying to negotiate the release of more than $6bn in Iranian assets, which could lead to the reopening of the strait of Hormuz and the restart of negotiations on Iran’s nuclear programme.

The United Arab Emirates envoy Anwar Gargash said that another round of escalation was not in the interests of Iran or any of its neighbours. But he added: “We are also, as we have shown before, braced for the worst.”
He added: “Relations with Iran are essential, because Iran is our neighbour and we do not want to see it get caught up in a prolonged crisis.”

Qatar’s mediation continued despite unidentified missiles striking a Pakistan-bound Qatari LNG tanker near the strait of Hormuz on Friday. The attack came despite the ship receiving direct clearance and safe-passage approval from Tehran just hours earlier.

In a bid to overcome the lack of trust on both sides, Qatar has been focusing its efforts on reaching an agreement for a plan to compress the process by which the US lifts sanctions, and then Iran reopens the strait of Hormuz and starts nuclear talks. Iran has agreed to cut the timetable from seven to two days,

blocks.caption: Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi. Photograph: Abedin Taherkenareh/EPA

blocks.text: Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said he hoped the US would choose “diplomacy over other paths”. He said Iran was ready for both defence and diplomacy, depending on Washington’s “rationality”. Araghchi said there were currently no plans for direct talks with Washington.
Araghchi has not been attending the mediation in Doha and is due to go to Turkmenistan on Monday, but other Iranian diplomats are heavily involved.
Donald Trump said on Saturday that the US had knocked out much of Iran’s military but still had to “take care of” one or two targets, as Tehran warned of reprisals if attacked.
Trump maintained that negotiations with Iran to end the war, which was started by the US and Israel in February, were “going fine but you know they’re not very reliable”.

Earlier on Saturday, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the US was open to a diplomatic solution, while Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, disclosed that he had received a letter from the US vice-president, JD Vance, seeking to revive talks.

blocks.caption: US secretary of state, Marco Rubio. Photograph: Erik S Lesser/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Rezaei noted what he described as a positive change in “tone” from the US side but said he had yet to respond.

Speaking to Al Jazeera on Saturday, Araghchi said Iran had offered to open the strait of Hormuz within two days of the US acting to lift the blockade on oil ships, stop blocking the release of Iranian assets and end sanctions on Iranian oil exports.

Ali Nikzad, the deputy speaker of Iran’s parliament, once again signalled that Tehran would be unwilling to discuss its nuclear programme, saying: “Our enemies must understand that the Iranian nation has made a decision not to negotiate on the nuclear issue under any circumstances or under any pressure. This great nation gave its enemies enough opportunity to negotiate in this area, but was faced with repeated breaches of promises and illegal bombing of part of peaceful nuclear facilities.”

Rezaei claimed Trump was being hounded by a war that he claimed was having wider international repercussions than the Vietnam war. He told Iranian TV on Saturday: “Today, wherever Trump goes, he must answer why he started the war against Iran. There is no family in America that has not endured the pressure caused by the war in Iran.”

articles.title: Democrat Haley Stevens endorses Abdul El-Sayed’s Republican rival Mike Rogers
articles.summary:
Stevens lost the party’s Michigan primary by a close margin and had refused to endorse El-Sayed, with tensions between the two high

Congresswoman Haley Stevens, who lost the Michigan…

blocks.text: Congresswoman Haley Stevens, who lost the Michigan Democratic Senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed, endorsed his Republican rival, Mike Rogers, in an extraordinary rebuke of her party’s nominee on the eve of the midterm elections.

Her endorsement came in a video posted to X after she attended an event with Rogers at the predominantly Black Perfecting church in Detroit on Sunday. The event marks a stunning political moment in Michigan, where control of the seat could be crucial to Democratic party.

Stevens had lost by a close margin in this year’s primary, and for months had refused to openly back El-Sayed, as had his other opponent Mallory McMorrow. But top Democrats had brokered the truce between El-Sayed and Stevens. After the two had sparred viciously in the primary campaign Stevens extended him a tepid endorsement, and this weekend was scheduled to join El-Sayed at a predominantly Black church in Detroit’s North End.
Those plans have quickly unraveled over an issue that divided Stevens and El-Sayed perhaps more than any other: Israel.

Later last week, Stevens, a staunch supporter of Israel, made clear that her appearance alongside El-Sayed was preconditioned on his denouncing of an outside group’s campaign ad that had blamed US support of Israel for the rising cost of living. El-Sayed declined the request, accusing Stevens of needlessly reopening debates from a settled primary.

As the feud escalated, El-Sayed’s campaign went further, formally disinviting Stevens from his campaign events in the closing days of the campaign. Debbie Dingell, a Michigan congresswoman, later told CNN she had been the one to tell Stevens “this isn’t working” when it came to Stevens’ appearance with El-Sayed on Sunday. Dingell added that the tensions between the two were a distraction and that “there’s nothing to be gained by the two of them being in the same place”.

Earlier on Sunday Stevens had put out a statement that said she expected El-Sayed to win and telling people to vote. But just hours later she appeared with Donald Trump’s Senate pick and in one comment said she supported Rogers’ purported future investment in Black businesses.
after newsletter promotion

As the vicious political firestorm has unfolded, Democratic commentators have also pointed out that Stevens’ fiance, Jason Turkish, has been condemning El-Sayed publicly while supporting Rogers. Turkish, who is also vocally pro-Israel, has donated heavily to Democrats in the past, but this year also donated to Republican candidates including Susan Collins.

articles.title: How Rachel Reeves has mapped out the agenda for Andy Burnham’s government
articles.summary: On Brexit, devolution and investment, the former chancellor is eerily in tune with the man who sacked her

blocks.text: Which senior politician has argued that “Brexit did deep damage” and that the government seeks “not to turn back the clock but to look toward a new and stable, future relationship?”

It was not Andy Burnham, who has been the torchbearer for thinking the unthinkable on Brexit since he became prime minister. Instead, these are the words of the former chancellor Rachel Reeves, in a lecture six months ago.
Reeves has taken a more thoughtful approach on how to come to terms with life outside government than some of her fellow former ministers.
A speech at Harvard on Monday will be her first public intervention on her own record and on Britain’s future, wisely left until after John Healey’s first budget.

She will say no one in government could “be in any doubt” about her view on the damage of Brexit – and her belief that one day the UK should return to the EU fold. “Economic interests, common values and basic geographical reality all point towards Europe,” Reeves will say.

The speech, which will examine how governments can meet the public’s appetite for radicalism while maintaining credibility with financial markets, will say that pursuing a closer relationship with the EU, even rejoining, may be credible as well as radical.

“Economically, it is the credible choice. Britain’s values, and a serious assessment of the geopolitical scene today, tell us it is the radical choice too,” she will say, giving Burnham “credit for his willingness to face reality head on”.

The Treasury, where the blueprints for the Remain campaign’s “Project Fear” were drawn up, has always been the heart of pro-European sentiment in government and Reeves its biggest champion under Keir Starmer.

Her sentiment seems more aligned though with that of Burnham, who cast her out of government, than with Healey, her successor as chancellor. He has joked about his own age when asked if the UK would rejoin the EU “in his lifetime”, saying it was his job to “try and make the most of Britain’s position now”.

Within Westminster, there are more than whispers from some MPs that they have judged Reeves’s legacy and influence too harshly. Healey’s first outing at the International Monetary Fund in Bangkok saw its economists lavish praise on his predecessor, saying the UK’s deficit reduction plan “stands out” among G7 peers.

It is particularly striking how the themes of Reeves’s lecture have become the agenda for Burnham’s government. In it, she argued: “Today, what most distinguishes Britain from our closest peers is the relative underperformance of our major cities outside London, compared to their European counterparts.”
Reeves, who is the MP for Leeds West and Pudsey, said the north of England had “waited for far too long, for a government that matches warm words with concerted ambition”.

Her call to “liberate our regions from stifling Whitehall orthodoxies” sounds strikingly Burnhamesque. The main policy announced in the speech? A plan to begin giving regional leaders a share of national taxes “which have, for too long, been allocated by central government”.

That work now forms the centrepiece of Healey’s budget. If this government has its own theory of growth – Brexit and devolution – it is awkward at best that it removed the key backer of both under Starmer.
But Reeves’s main theory of growth was investment, in pursuit of which she raised employers’ national insurance.

That is the other reason for Burnham’s government to be grateful to Reeves – and for which she has received no credit. Those tax raises – despite being unpopular – gave a sense of a government willing to make hard choices while taking the risk to borrow for public investment. The fiscal rules were changed to allow for a multi-year commitment to an eventual £100bn in new capital spending.

The cash is now beginning to flow into NHS infrastructure, roads, housing, rail upgrades and energy and industrial investments. Reeves will lay out her theory in her Harvard speech this week that the shift to an investment-led growth model “required sacrifices” that a Starmer-led government failed to get the public to back.
“The challenge is to make the politics and economics, those dual tests of credibility and radicalism, line up,” Reeves will say.
She will not say – although others have – that much of the problem with Starmer’s government was the man himself, rather than the agenda.

Burnham, if he avoids an early election, may start to see some of that investment bear fruit in public and market confidence, both in upgraded public services and in Britain’s appeal as a location for private investment.

There is much that could derail all this – not least further international turmoil – but when Burnham’s government counts its success on public services, Europe, devolution and growth, Reeves will be able to claim some credit.

articles.title: Police detain 325 people at pro-Palestine Action protest at US embassy in London
articles.summary:
Arrests come ahead of Wednesday’s supreme court challenge to the ban on the direct action group

Police have said they arrested 325 people on Saturday at

blocks.text: Police have said they arrested 325 people on Saturday at a demonstration outside the US embassy in London against the proscription of Palestine Action.

In updated arrest figures released on Sunday, the Metropolitan police said 320 people were detained outside the building in Battersea, south London, for allegedly expressing support for an organisation banned under the Terrorism Act.

The arrests came ahead of Wednesday’s supreme court challenge to the ban on Palestine Action – the first direct action group to be proscribed under the Terrorism Act – which came into effect on 5 July last year.

Defend Our Juries, which has organised the mass civil disobedience campaign against proscription, said Saturday’s detentions took the total number of people arrested for allegedly supporting Palestine Action since the ban to 4,200. Most arrests have been for holding placards reading “I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action.”

The overall number of detentions will probably feature in the hearing before the UK’s highest court, which was granted on the basis that it was arguable that the ban represents a disproportionate interference with the rights of freedom of speech and protest.

blocks.caption: Hundreds of protesters hold signs outside the US embassy in London on Saturday. Photograph: Martin Pope/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: However, neither the high court, which ruled that the ban was unlawful, nor the court of appeal, which overturned the high court’s decision, gave much weight to the fate of the placard-holders.

About 2,500 of those arrested for alleged support of Palestine Action have been charged under the Terrorism Act but all trials have been postponed pending a definitive decision on whether or not the ban was lawful.
Saturday’s demonstrations – there was also a vigil in Edinburgh, although Police Scotland made no arrests – were the largest, against the ban, of Andy Burnham’s premiership.

In September, when quizzed by LBC radio’s Andrew Marr about the “elderly people, vicars and grannies” who have been arrested for holding placards allegedly supporting Palestine Action, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, said: “I don’t think anyone’s intent was to have those people criminalised. But obviously the supreme court has got to look at this issue and obviously it’s something we keep looking at as a government.”

The following week, in an interview with The Rest is Politics podcast, Shabana Mahmood said it had been “very uncomfortable” to see some protesters arrested for alleged support of Palestine Action. Mahmood, the home secretary, nevertheless defended the ban.
The supreme court hearing will conclude on Thursday, with judgment reserved until a later date.

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy is back in court - where will her case go next?
articles.summary: The Massachusetts mother, accused of murdering her three children, is expected back in court as she awaits a decision on whether her case will be retried.

blocks.text: Fundamentally, Clancy's legal team - with Reddington at the helm - is pushing for the charges to be dismissed or dropped. They've explored a variety of legal avenues.

In September, he asked for her to be found not guilty under Rule 25 - a Massachusetts provision that states a defendant should be found not guilty if prosecutors do not present enough evidence at trial.
That request was denied.

Judge Sullivan will hear arguments on several motions on Monday, but Heather Cucolo, a New York Law School professor and mental health law expert, told the BBC that the hearing will likely focus on a narrow point: was this an instance of a routine deadlocked-jury mistrial - in which the jury genuinely could not agree - or was this an improperly terminated trial?
She said Reddington may argue that a retrial could violate Clancy's Constitutional protection against double jeopardy - a legal standard that says a person cannot be tried for the same crime twice.
But legal experts agree that outcome is unlikely.

"The public attention that's been put on this trial and the need to have some conclusion in the near future, I think that the judge is going to say that this mistrial was appropriate, was legally accurate, and that they need to now look to set a date for a retrial," Cucolo said.
Judge Sullivan could make a determination over whether the case can proceed on Monday or he could rule later in writing, criminal defence lawyer Elyse Hershon told the BBC.
And how the District Attorney's office wants to proceed could be determined ahead of Monday's hearing, during it or even days after, she said.
"The three charges of first-degree murder are still pending; they are still hanging over Lindsay Clancy's head unless and until the DA announces otherwise," Hershon said.
Historically, Cruz, the district attorney, has made comments and announcements about the case at press conferences after court finishes. That could happen again this week, she predicted.
It is also likely, Hershon said, that Judge Sullivan pushes the lawyers on both sides to get a trial date on the calendar during Monday's hearing.

"It does not mean it's definitely going to be a jury trial, but [they will want to] put something in the books, hold those dates. It's a big chunk of time. It's four, five, six weeks of the court calendar; that's hard to fit in at the last minute," she said.
"I would anticipate they block off the time while they go through all these motions and the DA's office figures out what it wants to do."

articles.title: Medical oncologist based in Brandon, Man., says he's leaving his 'dream job' over lack of support
articles.summary: A medical oncologist based in Brandon is leaving the role in November, saying his repeated calls for support have been ignored by the province.

image.caption: Dr. Brady Anderson's last day as a medical oncologist practising out of the Western Manitoba Cancer Centre in Brandon, Man., will be Nov. 13. (CancerCare Manitoba)

blocks.text: Manitoba
A medical oncologist based in Brandon is leaving the role in November, saying his repeated calls for support have been ignored by the province.
CancerCare promises continuity for western Manitoba patients

Dr. Brady Anderson has been practising out of the Western Manitoba Cancer Centre in Brandon for four years. His last day as a medical oncologist will be Nov. 13, at which point he will begin working as a hospitalist at the Brandon Regional Health Centre.
Anderson told CBC News on Friday it "has been quite devastating" to have to step away from oncology.
"This was my dream job since I was an early medical student," he said.
"I had several family members suffering from cancer, and I wanted to be able to come back and contribute to the region with something that was really needed. That was my biggest motivation."
On call by default
Anderson has been the sole medical oncologist outside of Winnipeg, he said. He said the workload, and a lack of support from both the province and CancerCare Manitoba, have led to his burnout.

The CancerCare site in Brandon continues to have two family doctors trained in oncology and three radiation oncologists. But when it comes to making major decisions for patients, diagnosis and major changes to treatment plans, the responsibility falls on Anderson, he said.
This has led to him being perpetually on call by default, he said.
"I'm effectively being forced into a significant amount of unpaid overtime, with no promise or guarantee that it will be fixed or compensated in the future," Anderson said.
Despite promises of support in the form of nurse practitioners, clinical assistants or physician assistants, nothing ever came to fruition, he said.

items: Province 'heading in the right direction' on physician shortages, but gaps remain: Doctors Manitoba

blocks.text: "What I've maintained the entirety of the last two years ... is that if the workload is necessary, then I'm willing to — at least until they recruit somebody else — provide it, but knowing that it's going to be compensated. If compensation can't be committed to, then something else at least needs to be taken off my plate," Anderson said.
"It's acknowledged, but the overwhelming response has been, 'Yeah, we really should do something about it.' But nothing ever happens."
At any given time, Anderson said he actively oversees the treatments and follow-ups of several hundred patients. He said his biggest concern is that there will be a care gap in the Westman area.
"That concern is what led me to stay in the position, despite many years of this frustration, for as long as I have," Anderson said.
Doctors Manitoba spokesperson Keir Johnson said in an email to CBC News that there are 23 medical oncologists listed as working in Manitoba, with only one in Brandon and the rest in Winnipeg.
"According to our analysis of national data, Manitoba has about 20 per cent fewer medical oncologists per capita than the Canadian average," Johnson wrote.
A spokesperson for the provincial government said another medical oncologist started approximately a month ago and will carry on Anderson's workload when he leaves.
Brandon West MLA Wayne Balcaen says Anderson's departure will 'impact thousands of people whose lives have been forever changed' because of cancer. (Jaison Empson/CBC)
Anderson, however, said he has been given "next to no information on the future coverage plans despite requesting repeatedly to be involved in it to make sure patients do not get lost."
"I have grave concerns about the sustainability of this, as presumably they will be tasked with virtually stepping into the same unsustainable workload," Anderson said.
Brandon West MLA Wayne Balcaen brought up Anderson's departure during Thursday's question period, saying it will "impact thousands of people whose lives have been forever changed" because of cancer.
"This is not just a Brandon problem, it's a Westman problem," Balcaen said, noting he's heard from constituents from across western Manitoba concerned with Anderson's departure.
"For many people, the only way to ensure they don't die, or to prolong their life, is to get timely treatment by a medically trained cancer doctor such as Dr. Anderson."

Health Minister Uzoma Asagwara at the Manitoba Legislature in March. The health minister says the province has been working with Prairie Mountain Health to recruit and retain more professionals. (Bryce Hoye/CBC)
Provincial Health Minister Uzoma Asagwara said during question period that the government has been working with Prairie Mountain Health to recruit and retain more professionals in the region.
"We recognize the challenges with staffing, and we're going to keep doing the work to make sure more residents of Prairie Mountain Health have access to the cancer care services they need."

Twylla Krueger, director of communications for CancerCare Manitoba, said in a written statement that Prairie Mountain Health and CancerCare are "committed to ensuring continuity of care for patients" in the Westman region.
"Following Dr. Anderson's departure, another medical oncologist will be assigned to provide care for patients at the Western Manitoba Cancer Centre," Krueger said.

"Patients will continue to receive care at their preferred CancerCare Manitoba location. Our clinical teams will work directly with patients to co-ordinate appointments and ensure a smooth transition, with no interruption to their ongoing care."
Brandon Mayor Jeff Fawcett reiterated that Westman shouldn't see any disruption.

items: Manitoba will hire up to 90 family doctors by 2029 with $6M in federal funding: health minister

blocks.text: "We realized [Brandon] is the medical hub for the region, and so we do need to make sure that we can have specialists here," he said.
"Recruitment is one thing, and retention is the other. It's the community that makes retention easier."
Anderson, who was born and raised in Westman, said he is glad to remain in Brandon and provide the services he can.
"He is an asset, in that he's working as a hospitalist, and that helps. We need that as well," the mayor said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Erin DeBooy is a reporter with CBC Manitoba. Born and raised in Winnipeg, she has experience reporting in the city and across the province. She has previously worked with the Brandon Sun, covering a wide range of topics including courts, education, arts and breaking news. She can be reached at erin.debooy@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Ukraine defies Trump to resume attacks on Russian oil
articles.summary:
Reported strikes on two refineries risk angering the US president days before his country’s midterm elections

Ukraine has resumed its attacks on Russian oil refineries in defiance of…

blocks.text: Ukraine has resumed its attacks on Russian oil refineries in defiance of pressure from Donald Trump ahead of the US midterm elections, with a ceasefire in the occupied town of Oleshky due to end late on Sunday.

Russian state media said on Sunday Ukrainian long-range drones had set fire to the Kstovo refinery in Nizhny Novgorod oblast overnight, following soon after a major strike against another big refinery in Samara oblast, owned by the Russian state energy giant Rosneft.
The Wall Street Journal had reported that Ukraine had given in to pressure from the White House to stop bombing Russian energy infrastructure.

Ukrainian officials, however, told the Kyiv Independent newspaper that they never agreed to a demand from Jared Kushner, the US president’s son-in-law, to pause refinery strikes for 30 days. The raids on restarted on Friday, Kremlin officials said, complaining that Kyiv is now “simply ignoring” US wishes.
Trump has blamed the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, for the rise in global fuel prices, and last month lifted US sanctions on Russian diesel.

Zelenskyy has not acknowledged the latest refinery attacks, in an apparent attempt to avoid angry US reprisals. Instead, he said his armed forces had hit a defence industry enterprise in Russia’s Rostov region that made missiles. A Pantsir missile system was destroyed, he added, as part of Ukraine’s ongoing “long-range sanctions”.

Zelenskyy said that his country was obliged to retaliate because of a remorseless campaign by Moscow, using drones and ballistic missiles, against vulnerable city-based energy facilities. Four regions were hit by Russia overnight, with electricity cut as a result in hundreds of thousands of households.

“The intensity of the strikes is very high, and the Russians are seeking to maximally exploit the ​deficit of ballistic missile interceptors,” the Ukrainian president said on Telegram. Kyiv experienced power cuts lasting eight to ten hours on Sunday, after a critical thermal power plant was damaged.

Zelenskyy said Russia was suffering record losses, with 54,400 military personnel killed and wounded in October – the highest monthly figure since the full-scale war began. He said Ukraine recaptured 96.2 sqkm (37 sq miles) of its territory last month, 10.4 sqkm (4 sq miles) more than Moscow managed to seize, and emphasised: “Russia is losing.”

The latest attacks came as a six-day local ceasefire brokered by the US first lady, Melania Trump, was due to come to an end in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky. Hundreds of residents were reunited with their loved ones over the weekend in northern Ukraine, with both sides hailing the evacuation mission as a success.

Ukrainian observers say the Russian military used the truce to reinforce its positions and to swap hungry and exhausted troops garrisoned in Oleskhy. The town sits on the left bank of the Dnipro River, to the east, and is opposite the larger city of Kherson, which Ukraine recaptured in autumn 2022. A renewed Russian onslaught is inevitable, the observers believe.
after newsletter promotion
The pope said on Sunday he hoped cooperation between ⁠Russia and Ukraine in implementing the Oleshky ceasefire – the most significant since 2022 – would ⁠pave the ⁠way ​for broader peace efforts.
“I hope that the cooperation between the parties, which made this necessary humanitarian gesture possible, will strengthen their willingness to engage in dialogue,” he said during his Sunday prayer.

Trilateral talks involving Russia, Ukraine and the US are likely to take place later this month, with Kremlin officials saying on Sunday that Putin was willing to talk directly with Zelenskyy by phone. They added that European leaders who support Ukraine should not be involved in any such call.

There is little prospect of a wider breakthrough, however, as the Russian president’s maximalist demands remain unchanged. He is insisting that Ukraine give up all of the eastern Donetsk oblast – which Russia has been unable to seize since 2014 – as well as further territory in Kherson and Zaporizhzhia provinces, which the Kremlin does not control but says it has “annexed”.

articles.title: Serbia: Police chief arrested after election for abuse of office
articles.summary: Marko Kricak, an Aleksandar Vucic loyalist, is accused of suppressing and manipulating an investigation into a gangland murder. Prosecutors say the arrest is not linked to Vucic's recent election…

image.caption: Prosecutors say the arrest is not linked to Vucic's recent election defeat.Image: Mitar Mitrovic/REUTERS

blocks.text: The head of Serbia's criminal police directorate has been arrested and charged with abuse of office, state media reported on Sunday.
Marko Kricak is accused of suppressing and manipulating an investigation into the murder in May of a suspected criminal underworld figure in a Belgrade restaurant.
Serbia: who is police chief Marko Kricak?

The 42-year-old was seen as a supporter of defeated Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic, whose right-wing populist camp was defeated by the opposition Student List in parliamentary elections on October 25.
Indeed, he has also been accused by student groups of "brutality" in the police response to peaceful anti-Vucic demonstrations.
The removal of Kricak and other Vucic loyalists in Serbia's police and intelligence apparatus was one of student leaders' demands.
But Belgrade's chief prosecutor, Nenad Stefanovic, denied a connection between the student movement's demands and Kricak's arrest.
"This arrest has no link with ... the result of the legislative elections," he told journalists.
Against all odds: How Serbia's students took on Vucic
Serbia: Vucic system dismantled
Nevertheless, the arrest of a senior police officer regarded as close to the former regime is being seen as an example of the strongholds of the Vucic system slowly eroding.
Kricak worked as a car salesman before being recruited into Serbia's domestic intelligence agency, the BIA, and was a loyal supporter of Vucic's Serbian Progressive Party (SNS).
In July 2023, he was appointed commander of the Serbian police's personal protection unit (JZO).

It was in this position that he is alleged to have personally led the abduction of a group of university students, allegedly assaulting one female student and threatening to rape her in the basement of a government building in Belgrade.
At the end of 2025, he was appointed head of the Serbian Criminal Police.

articles.title: National Grid to site biggest substation on Teesside, near planned AI datacentre
articles.summary:
New electricity generating capacity would enable north-east to attract investment for major datacentre projects

National Grid has taken a step towards building Britain’s biggest electricity…

blocks.text: National Grid has taken a step towards building Britain’s biggest electricity substation on Teesside, which could supply power to a vast neighbouring datacentre, as the UK races to expand its AI infrastructure.
Last week the company agreed to purchase 73 acres of land at Dorman Point on a site owned by Teesworks, a local private-public partnership. The deal was first reported by Sky News.

The deal follows reports last year that the UK government had picked Teesworks as the site for a new artificial intelligence datacentre, and planning applications had been submitted for a project of nearly 500,000 sq metres.

Matt Pearce, the head of land at National Grid, said the deal “reflects the constructive work between all those involved to enable this vital infrastructure … and will support the growth of AI and digital technologies, and enable the region’s next phase of industrial and economic development.
“We are committed to working closely with our partners to progress the development as quickly as possible,” he said.

Ben Houchen, the Tees Valley combined authority mayor, told Sky News: “Everyone who has tried to build a datacentre in this country knows the biggest problem is getting enough power to the site quickly.

blocks.caption: Ben Houchen, the Tees Valley mayor. Photograph: Mark Pinder/The Guardian

blocks.text: “While we’ve been stuck in the queue, the US, the Gulf and parts of Europe have been getting on with it and hoovering up the investment. Having up to 3.2GW of capacity here means we can finally compete for those projects.

“If Britain is serious about having its own AI capability, with sensitive data stored safely on British soil, it needs somewhere to physically put it, and I’d much rather that was Teesside than Texas or Abu Dhabi.”

Last week the government published a draft national policy statement on datacentres, describing them as “as fundamental to our economy as the railways and electricity networks on which we have long depended”.
“We must take control over the development of datacentres in this country and ensure that the country and host communities benefit from them,” it said.

However the rapid construction of datacentres in the UK has triggered opposition, with campaign groups protesting against planned developments in places ranging from Auchtertool, a village north of Edinburgh, to Brick Lane in east London.

In October, the Guardian reported that AI companies told ministers they had 12 months to head off public opposition to datacentres in the UK or risk US-style protests that could threaten their construction.

Balfour Beatty, the London-listed infrastructure services group, was reported to be in line to deliver the Teesworks substation for National Grid, with Steel River Power (SRP) also heavily involved in the project.
Balfour Beatty and SRP were approached for comment.
