articles.title: University of Cambridge scientist among those who died in Spanish train crash
articles.summary: Marta Shahbazi was an "inspiring, talented and passionate scientist", says the laboratory where she worked.

blocks.text: An award-winning University of Cambridge researcher died in the Spanish train disaster while on her way to collect a prize for scientific excellence.
Dr Marta Shahbazi was travelling to an awards ceremony on Wednesday when the train she was on crashed into another near Urda, south of Madrid, killing 69 people.

The mother of two was an affiliate associate professor leading a group of researchers at MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology (LMB) in Cambridge and had earned several awards for work on human embryos and cell biology.
In a statement, the LMB paid tribute to the "inspiring, talented and passionate scientist" and described her death as a "profound shock and a huge loss".
The expert in cell biology ran the Shahbazi Laboratory at the LMB, based on the Cambridge Biomedical Campus.

She had been announced as the winner of a Spanish Society for Developmental Biology award for her contributions to the study of early human development and was due to collect the award at a conference in El Rompido in Andalusia.

The LMB said: "As a wife and mother of two young children, Marta wrote eloquently about balancing her family and career, serving as a much-admired role model for a 'mother scientist', a term she used to describe herself.

"Marta was an inspiring, talented and passionate scientist whose research shed light on the earliest steps in the development of human embryos and how errors occur that lead to failed pregnancies," the LMB said.
The institute said her death was "a profound shock and a huge loss for LMB".
Her work had been recognised with "many awards and prizes", the laboratory added.
Shahbazi is listed on the University of Cambridge website as a principal investigator at its Stem Cell Institute (CSCI).
Institute director Prof Bertie Gottgens said its community was "shocked and deeply saddened" by her death.

"Marta led her primary research group at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology (LMB) alongside her roles as an affiliate principal investigator and affiliate assistant professor at the CSCI," he said.
"Across both institutes, she was highly respected for her pioneering research on early human development and valued for her collaborative spirit.
"Her creativity, passion, and generosity will be greatly missed."
The news of her death was first confirmed in a social media post, external by the CiMUS, based in Santiago de Compostela where Shahbazi's aunt works.
Shahbazi undertook her PhD at the Spanish National Cancer Research Centre, before joining the University of Cambridge as a post-doctoral fellow and then the LMB in 2020.
The crash in Spain happened when a state-operated Renfe high-speed train smashed into the back of a stationary train operated by the Iryo company.
It is one of the worst rail disasters in Europe's modern history, and Spain's worst crash since 2013.
Three days of national mourning were declared in the country.
More than 540 people were on board both trains.

articles.title: UK willing to spend £450m a year on EU students if it can join Made in Europe scheme
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Plan to allow students from bloc pay same fees as Britons contingent on entry to industrial programme, officials say

Ministers are prepared to spend as much as £450m a year to…
articles.byline: Kiran Stacey, Lisa O’Carroll and Jessica Elgot

blocks.text: Ministers are prepared to spend as much as £450m a year to give students from the EU discounted university fees, the Guardian has learned, but only if Brussels allows the UK access to its Made in Europe industrial programme.

The UK government has drawn up plans to allow students arriving from the continent pay the same fees as British students, sources say, and is willing to spend hundreds of millions of pounds compensating universities to do so.

British officials insist, however, they will only make concessions on fees if the EU allows Britain entry to its proposed protectionist industrial scheme, which will impose trade restrictions on countries outside the bloc.

On Sunday the former chancellor Rachel Reeves praised the prime minister, Andy Burnham, for a willingness to think boldly about the UK’s relationship with Europe – saying she believed Britain’s future was within the EU. But in her first major intervention since leaving the Treasury when Burnham took office, she said those forging a path back towards EU membership had to make compelling arguments to the public.

Ministers hope if such an agreement is reached at a Brussels summit later this month it will unlock millions of pounds’ worth of benefits for British companies looking to do business in the EU, and show that the prime minister’s attempts to forge much closer ties with the bloc are paying off.
But giving EU students cheaper access to British universities could prove controversial domestically, especially when many graduates are calling for changes to their own student loan repayment plans.

One person with knowledge of the talks said: “We are willing to give the Europeans what they want on fees, but we will have to get something significant in return. The biggest prize we are pushing for right now is access to Made in Europe, so there is a deal to be done there.”

blocks.caption: Andy Burnham with the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, in September. Photograph: Toby Melville/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: A government spokesperson said: “We are building an ambitious, close relationship with the EU that will strengthen our economy, protect British industry, and create more opportunities for young people across the UK.”

Negotiators have been thrashing out a series of deals for months to be finalised at the long-awaited summit on 20 November. Burnham wants to use it to show his commitment to much closer ties with the EU and to lay out options for how the relationship could develop in the future, including full re-entry.

In a speech at Harvard on Monday, Reeves will say the UK’s “economic interests, common values and basic geographical reality all point towards Europe”. Praising Burnham’s “willingness to face reality head-on”, she will say it is vital the British government can “prove to the public the benefits of a closer relationship and prove to Europe that we are serious and open to compromise”.

Before the summit, agreement is understood to have largely been reached in a number of areas, including on emissions trading, agricultural products and a youth mobility scheme, with reports suggesting up to 80,000 young Europeans could be allowed to come to Britain to work, live and study. EU member states had demanded between 100,000 and 150,000, with some arguing in favour of no quota.
The two sides are also nearing agreement to allow Britain access to European biometric databases, the Guardian has learned, which could help the UK government track asylum seekers.
British access to the Made in Europe scheme, which is due to be finalised next year, and European demands for cheaper fees for students at British universities are the two remaining hurdles.

EU officials say they want their students to pay fees of just over £9,000 a year rather than international fees, which can rise above £60,000. The demand briefly brought negotiations to a standstill this year, with British officials saying they had been blindsided by its inclusion in talks.

The first draft of a joint statement will be presented to EU ambassadors on Wednesday with room for text to be added or deleted up to 20 November. The agreement will include fresh commitments to strengthen efforts to end the small boat crossings in the Channel, including commitments to explore the possibility of restoring the UK’s access to EU databases.
after newsletter promotion

EU diplomats say top of the UK’s shopping list is access to Eurodac, an EU database that holds fingerprints of all asylum seekers from the age of six. But they also warn there will be challenges for the UK as the database was not built for law enforcement, and sharing data with a non-EU member may not be supported by all states.

Member states are pushing for firm language on fees while the UK holds out for guarantees on Made in Europe. France dropped its opposition to the inclusion of the UK in the Industrial Accelerator Act with a proposal any country in the single market on 1 January 2020 could be involved as along as it dynamically aligned on trade measures.

Ten days ago, with talks still deadlocked, the EU discussed “decoupling” the discussion on fees from the joint statement at the summit entirely, deferring any agreement for six months. But EU diplomats still hope for an agreement to allow talks to flourish for what one called “the real reset”.

Sources have told the Guardian the government is willing to concede on fees and is prepared to pay cash-strapped universities for the income they will lose. Treasury officials have been drawing up estimates for how much such a policy will cost under various scenarios, including different levels of discounts for European students and different levels of demand for British university courses.

Two sources who have seen the costings have told the Guardian that under the most expensive scenario, which involves reducing fees to the same level as domestic students’ and very high levels of demand, the government could end up paying £450m a year. Another source said the true cost was likely to be lower, while a government official described the figure as “speculative”.

Mark Corver, an analyst of university funding and director at Campus Numerics, previously calculated it would cost the sector £140m in the first year and £400m across the three-year period of a typical course.
UK negotiators are only willing to give way on fees if they get a guarantee that British companies will be treated the same as those from the EU under the new industrial scheme.

The UK was excluded from the definition of “European” for the purposes of the scheme, prompting warnings from the British government and the UK car industry. More recently, however, France – which was the principal opponent of Britain’s inclusion in the scheme – shifted its position with a new proposal to allow British manufacturers into the system as long as the UK accepted “dynamic alignment” on EU tariffs.

This could cause a problem for the UK, which has much lower tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles than in the EU. Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, recently told the Guardian he would not set tariff policy in response to pressure from Brussels.

The UK is also working on securing access to the Schengen Information System II – a database holding records of fugitives, missing persons and stolen goods, which gives real-time alerts on their cross-border movements.

The EU commissioner responsible for migration, Magnus Brunner, had been due to meet the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, in London two weeks ago to flesh out that text, but after a last-minute cancellation, work has continued between officials at the Cabinet Office and the European Commission.

articles.title: Israeli strikes in Gaza kill eight including child, hospitals say
articles.summary: Five officers from the Hamas-run police have been killed in Khan Younis and three people, including a child, killed in Gaza City, officials say.

blocks.text: Israeli strikes in Gaza have killed at least eight people, including a child, according to hospitals, despite a year-old ceasefire.
In Gaza City to the north, hospital officials said a missile attack hit a group of civilians next to Cairo School in the Al-Rimal neighbourhood, killing three people, including a child.

In the southern city of Khan Younis, the Hamas-run ministry of interior said a drone attack targeted a group of police officers in the Al-Mawasi area, killing five, as they were carrying out their routine duties.
The Israeli military said it had carried out two attacks on what it described as military operatives but has not yet provided evidence or further information.
The interior ministry named the five police officers killed, who were between the ages of 23 and 53. The ministry called the attack a "horrific massacre" by Israeli forces.
A ceasefire came into force in Gaza in October last year, but Israeli air strikes have continued almost every day.

Since then, 1,580 people have been killed, according to Gaza's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. Israel says it is targeting Hamas, but often civilians are also killed.
Meanwhile, a peace plan for Gaza, brokered by the Trump administration, has stalled.

The ceasefire saw thousands of Palestinians held by Israel released in return for all of the 48 remaining hostages held in Gaza, and an agreement to end the war - which was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage.
Since the war began, 74,594 people have been killed in Gaza, according to the territory's health ministry.
Additional reporting by Jacob Phillips

articles.title: Attempted murder probe after petrol bomb thrown at French riot police
articles.summary:
Youth-led protests end with street violence in cities across France, Germany, Switzerland, Portugal and Albania

French officials have opened an investigation into the attempted murder of a…

blocks.text: French officials have opened an investigation into the attempted murder of a police officer and Germany’s interior minister has called for harsh penalties after peaceful and mainly youth-led protests across Europe ended in violence.
In Portugal, police – some with dogs – cleared protest camps with baton charges, while security forces in Switzerland were attacked with paving stones.
Protests over the education system, deteriorating public services, declining prospects, unaffordable housing and the spiralling cost of living have shaken a number of countries this autumn.

Violence erupted in the French capital as well as Marseille, Grenoble, Bordeaux, Lyon and Toulouse on Saturday night after an estimated 320,000 demonstrators, some in Halloween costume, took to the streets.

blocks.caption: Protesters in Halloween costumes gather in the La Plaine square in Marseille. Officials say 320,000 people took part in protests across France. Photograph: Sener Yilmaz Aslan/Getty Images

blocks.text: As the rallies ended, masked and hooded rioters arrived and caused what the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, described as an “extraordinary” level of violence. More than 770 people were arrested.

In Paris, the prosecutor’s office said incendiary devices were thrown at a group of about 15 gendarmes and police officers and a formal investigation had been opened for “attempted murder of persons vested with public authority”.
Injuries reportedly included second-degree burns in an incident captured on mobile phone video and shared on social media and broadcast on French television.

blocks.caption: A protester in a Batman costume salutes in front of a fire started by rioters in Frankfurt. German authorities have promised a strong response. Photograph: Kai Pfaffenbach/Reuters

blocks.text: The level of physical violence and looting was significantly lower than on 17 October, when 2,600 people were arrested and as many as 3,000 shops pillaged in one of the worst nights of urban unrest in France’s recent history.
In Germany, looters and rioters ⁠rampaged through Frankfurt, the country’s financial hub, damaging stores and injuring more than 100 police officers.

“The rioters and looters will be identified and held accountable,” said Alexander Dobrindt, the hardline interior minister. He singled out “violent left-wing groups and troublemakers from the migrant community”, adding: “Tough penalties must follow this breach of the peace.”

blocks.caption: Riot police clear Lisbon’s Rossio Square of activists protesting over housing affordability. Photograph: Manuel de Almeida/EPA

blocks.text: Dobrindt told the tabloid newspaper Bild that deploying a heavy police presence across multiple locations had been effective. “Excesses of ​violence like those ‌in Paris were ​prevented thanks to our ​highly committed police forces,” he said.
More than 100,000 protesters marched in over 30 German cities on Saturday to demand better ⁠education and lower living costs in protests led by the “Gen Z regelt” (Gen Z will sort it) campaign.
Hooded rioters ⁠damaged 17 Frankfurt shops, looting five of them, and threw missiles including petrol bombs, according to Roman Poseck, the state interior minister for Hesse.

More than 100 of the 1,300 police officers deployed in the city were injured and 54 suspects, ‌aged from 13 to 29, were arrested. “I am shocked by what I have seen, and there is no point in sugar-coating it. Let me make this very clear: things cannot go on like this,” Poseck said.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: An anti-government protest in Tirana turned violent with protesters hurling stones and petrol bombs at police. Photograph: Vlasov Sulaj/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Most of those arrested were German nationals, the minister said, adding that police estimated they had been confronted with “between 1,000 and 1,500 violent troublemakers, predominantly from a migrant background”.

Violence also broke out Saturday night in Cologne, where police used water cannon to disperse the crowd, and in Berlin, where protesters attacked police with bottles and fireworks. Gen Z regelt posted a statement distancing itself from all violence.

In Portugal, riot police removed protesters by force from Rossio Square in Lisbon at about 4.30am on Sunday after thousands of people angry at the housing crisis marched through the city on Saturday and set up camp.

blocks.caption: Protesters in Halloween costumes at an unauthorised demonstration in Marseille over the high cost of living. Photograph: Coust Laurent/ABACA/Shutterstock

blocks.text: The protesters want Portugal’s minority centre-right government to withdraw a ⁠bill that makes ⁠evictions easier and ends rent caps on new leases. A smaller camp in Porto was also cleared by force.

In Albania, masked protesters hurled stones and firebombs at police in the capital, Tirana, on the margins of a demonstration demanding the resignation of the prime minister, Edi Rama, over perceived corruption.

Youths threw paving stones and firebombs at police and set fire to rubbish bins at the end of a largely peaceful protest. The interior ministry said on Friday that 350 people had been hurt in the protests, including 200 police, with 269 minors arrested.

blocks.caption: Riot police in action in Paris. Almost 800 people were arrested across France for public order offences. Photograph: Bernard Jules/ABACA/Shutterstock

blocks.text: In Switzerland, hundreds of protesters gathered in Zürich and Basel on Saturday night for unauthorised demonstrations – both of which ended in violence – under the slogan: “We’ve had enough in Switzerland, too.”

In Zürich, police used water cannon, teargas and rubber bullets to disperse rioters attacking them with fireworks, bottles and stones, Swiss media reported. A police patrol car was damaged and rubbish bins and electric bikes set on fire.

In Basel, police said about 150 people gathered in the city centre at around 9pm. Shop windows were smashed, facades tagged with graffiti and bins and bikes set on fire, with incidents also reported in Geneva.

articles.title: Animal welfare group seeks nationwide probe into pet crematorium services
articles.summary: Animal welfare advocates have urged government agencies and organizations to investigate the operations of pet cremation services across the country.

blocks.text: Published November 2, 2026 12:04am
Animal welfare advocates have urged government agencies and organizations to investigate the operations of pet cremation services across the country.

"The reported discovery of the remains of deceased companion animals allegedly dumped instead of being cremated has raised serious concerns about the integrity of pet cremation services in the country," said the Philippine Animal Welfare Society (PAWS) in a statement.
PAWS is calling on the appropriate agencies to investigate the establishment involved in the incident and other pet crematoria operating in other parts of the country.

It was reported on Saturday that the decomposing remains of more than 20 dogs and cats were found sealed in plastic bags and dumped along New Town Street in Barangay Minuyan Proper, San Jose del Monte City, Bulacan.
The next day, authorities have retrieved and identified the remains of 22 dogs and three cats that were dumped.
According to the report of GMA News' Gabriel Gonzales, the remains were immediately placed inside body bags. Their names and weight were also indicated.
There were some fur parents who personally claimed the remains of their late fur babies.

"Following reports of deceased companion animals allegedly dumped instead of being cremated, PAWS is calling for a nationwide investigation of pet crematoria to ensure that these establishments operate lawfully, transparently, and with accountability," the group said.

The group called on various government agencies including the Department of Interior and Local Government (DILG), the Department of Health (DOH), the Philippine National Police (PNP), and the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) "to investigate possible violations involving business permits, sanitation, environmental regulations, consumer protection, criminal laws, and ensure that affected pet parents have access to appropriate legal remedies."

"Pet parents deserve the assurance that the cremation services they pay for are actually performed and that their beloved companions are treated with dignity even after death. The trust of grieving pet parents must never be exploited," PAWS also said. — BAP, GMA News

articles.title: Philippines, UAE partnership for oil storage facility sought
articles.summary: The government is courting the United Arab Emirates to build a strategic oil storage facility that can transform the Philippines into a regional energy hub and cushion domestic consumers from global…

blocks.text: November 2, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — The government is courting the United Arab Emirates to build a strategic oil storage facility that can transform the Philippines into a regional energy hub and cushion domestic consumers from global price volatility.

Senate energy committee chairman Erwin Tulfo pitched the government-to-government cooperation during bilateral talks on Oct. 29 with officials from the Abu Dhabi National Oil Co. (ADNOC), led by its chairman, Sultan Ahmed-Al Jaber.

“We have been pushing for this strategic oil hub as we see how beneficial it will be for Filipinos who are currently experiencing price shocks brought by high oil prices, because we lack access to it,” Tulfo told the UAE delegation.
ADNOC, which currently supplies Petron with approximately 40,000 barrels per day, expressed its willingness to advance the partnership.

To expedite discussions, the UAE delegation proposed sharing an existing storage contract framework for the Philippine government’s review, noting that a regional hub could significantly boost supply volumes.

Both parties identified a target rollout for the second quarter of 2027, pending final agreements on the facility’s location, infrastructure responsibilities, commercial terms and implementation schedule.

The proposed storage facility is expected to anchor a broader bilateral energy pact that would eventually cover crude supply agreements, refinery investments, fuel retail networks, gas-to-power development and renewable energy.
Tulfo said that while the deal is not yet final, he would shepherd subsequent meetings to secure the partnership.

MANILA, Philippines — President Marcos should take clear and concrete steps to arrest the peso’s continued depreciation against the US dollar and prevent the further erosion of Filipino’s buying power through soaring inflation with meager salaries, according to Akbayan party-list Rep. Chel Diokno.

He noted that while reassuring the public is important, Filipinos also need to see how the government intends to manage the economic challenges and mitigate the effects of rising prices on household budgets.

“Filipino families are already stretching their incomes to cover basic needs. The government must lay out clear, concrete measures to address these economic pressures and ease the burden on ordinary households,” he said.

MANILA, Philippines — As Sen. Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa continues to ignore an ultimatum for him to peacefully surrender, authorities were cautioned yesterday against publicizing details of ongoing efforts to capture the lawmaker.

“SSSHHH… : When pursuing a high-profile target or handling a sensitive live case, secrecy discipline is key – unless disinformation is necessary to flush the quarry into the open,” Lacson said in a social media post yesterday.

The former Philippine National Police chief issued the reminder to law enforcement agencies as operations against his former subordinate intensified following the lapse of a one-week surrender ultimatum on Friday.
Lacson said sensitive details should only be leaked to the public if it serves as a calculated strategy to draw the target out of hiding.

articles.title: Filipino artworks to ignite Spain’s Prado Museum
articles.summary: The single largest collection of works by Filipino old masters will wow the world when it opens at Spain’s national museum, the Prado, in November 2027. Conceived by the Prado itself, the…

blocks.text: November 2, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — The single largest collection of works by Filipino old masters will wow the world when it opens at Spain’s national museum, the Prado, in November 2027. Conceived by the Prado itself, the exhibit will showcase more than 70 Filipino works of the 19th century – and will be the first-ever of its kind.

The Prado is one of the globe’s greatest art museums, with a priceless collection of Velasquez, El Greco and Goya. The exhibition will finally give Philippine art its richly deserved place alongside that renowned company. The prestige conferred will be incalculable and underlines the country’s largely untapped soft power in art and culture.

A high-level mission led by the museum director, Miguel Falomir, is in Manila now as part of the last stages of preparation. With him is Francisco Tardio, the Prado’s global head for international relations.

Seven years in the making, the show will be curated by Carlos Navarro, the institution’s art historian and 19th-century specialist. The Filipino masterworks represent “a most important legacy that speaks to the complex, and at times, difficult history shared by Spain and the Philippines,” said Navarro.

All but one or two of these masterpieces have not been seen by the public in the Prado since 1898, when the Spanish empire in the Philippines ended, and the works were removed from exhibition walls or put into storage as a symbolic protest.

After almost a century and a half, the Prado will finally bring them back together to recreate a long-lost time when Filipino artists brought glory to their home country by earning Spain’s highest accolades.

The last quarter of the 19th century was the high tide of Filipino art, in terms of artistic excellence and its impact on the international stage, driven by the genius and charisma of its major figure, Juan Luna.

Luna, however, was not an isolated case but was a part of a broader movement known as the ilustrados (or the educated elite). Jose Rizal was an important part of that group and took inspiration from Luna.

“These young men cultivated themselves in the arts, literature, and sciences – including medicine and ethnography – with the utmost commitment to excellence. Their ambition extended well beyond personal advancement: it was, above all, the assertion of a collective Filipino presence at the highest levels within the cosmopolitan circuits of the Spanish Empire,” Navarro explains.

The exhibition will also spotlight many of the unsung heroes of Philippine art of that period. Among these, says Navarro, “Lorenzo Guerrero stands out – not only as a painter of great sensitivity, but also as a formative teacher and mentor to a whole generation of Filipino artists. Alongside him, figures such as Miguel Zaragoza and Melecio Figueroa will also be represented. Their contributions to painting and sculpture, respectively, are of exceptional merit.”

The landmark show has received the enthusiastic support of Falomir, the Prado’s director – whose leadership, throughout the project’s many years of gestation, reflects a keen sensitivity to postcolonial discourses and a renewed attention to the art of the Hispanic world. Slated for Autumn 2027, painstaking restoration is already underway to prepare the works so they can be viewed in as original a condition as when they were created.

The breakthrough show will be followed a year later by a second exhibit combining important paintings from Filipino collectors, making it a doubly significant international platform for Philippine art.

“To revisit this era is to rediscover a time of remarkable creativity and ambition, when Filipino artists engaged with the world and, in doing so, helped shape a new sense of identity and possibility for their nation. It is a story that continues to move and inspire us today,” said Navarro.

“The exhibitions offer unique opportunities to explore the work of Filipino artists as perhaps the world’s first transnational figures, whose lives and art were shaped by movement, exchange, and dialogue across cultures,” he added.

The show will also mark the 80th year of Philippine-Spanish diplomatic relations. The landmark show is in cooperation with the Spanish embassy in Manila, the Philippine embassy in Spain, the National Museum of the Philippines, and the National Commission for Culture and the Arts.

articles.title: Cardinal slams AI use to bring back the dead
articles.summary: As the nation remembers the dead, Pablo Virgilio Cardinal David of Kalookan has raised questions on the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in creating images that seem to bring the dead back to life.

blocks.text: November 2, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — As the nation remembers the dead, Pablo Virgilio Cardinal David of Kalookan has raised questions on the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in creating images that seem to bring the dead back to life.
In a Facebook post on Saturday, David likened the use of apps “AI Afterlife” or “AI HereAfter” as a scene from a horror movie that has turned into reality.
“Perhaps the real question this Halloween is no longer whether ghosts exist, but whether we are beginning to manufacture our own,” he said.

The Kalookan prelate said there are reportedly funeral services in the United States that offer to create the likeness of a person that talks, thinks and answers the same way as the departed, and uses a cloned voice of the deceased.

Through the service, AI is reportedly fed with the deceased person’s diaries, photographs, blogs, videos, voice recordings and other personal information. AI would then recreate a remarkably lifelike digital version of the departed – one the family can continue talking to, even years after the burial.

“Imagine attending a wake. After the eulogies, the deceased himself appears on a screen, speaking in his familiar voice, thanking the mourners by name, even chatting with his children and grandchildren!” David said.
But while some might find being able to talk to a deceased relative comforting, there are others that might view it as “downright creepy.”

“But here’s what troubles me: Are we preserving the memory of our loved ones, or creating an illusion that they have never really died? Could this technology help us grieve – or prevent us from learning to let go?” the cardinal added.

The Federation of Asian Bishops’ Conferences Office of Social Communications (FABC-OSC) is urging bishops conferences in the region to adopt AI safeguards and strengthen support for digital missionaries.

In a news story posted on CBCPNews, the FABC-OSC said in a statement that it is pushing for the creation of pastoral AI policies, digital literacy programs and authentic Church resources in local languages.

“(We) encourage episcopal conferences to establish pastoral safeguards for the use of AI appropriate to their context in line with the teachings of the Church,” said the statement, signed by FABC-OSC chairman Bishop Marcelino Antonio Maralit Jr., who is also the bishop of the Diocese of San Pablo, Laguna.
They also intend to establish a regional committee to train and support digital missionaries, whose work should be integrated into the Church’s evangelization mission.

The statement also warned of digital threats, including online sexual exploitation, cyber scams, deepfakes and unequal access to technology, as well as exploited labor and environmental damage linked to AI.
Prayers most important
Aside from offering flowers and lighting candles, praying for the dearly departed is the best way to remember them, according to a priest.

Fr. Vicente Gabriel Bautista, vice rector of the Manila Cathedral, said, “The best way to extend our love to the faithful departed is to offer the Holy Eucharist for them, to pray for them. Nothing tops that.”
He explained that candles and flowers are “outward expressions of love and closeness” to people we cherish and remember, “But at the top of everything, nothing beats offering masses and prayers.”

MANILA, Philippines — The Commission on Elections (Comelec) has approved the registration of a new local political party in Biñan, Laguna and the change of names and acronyms of two political groups ahead of the 2028 national and local elections.

In its rulings dated Oct. 29, the Comelec granted the petition of Lapiang Unlad Biñan (LUB), allowing it to register as a local political party in the city with all the rights accorded to such groups.

articles.title: Philippines welcomes US MRF-SEA deployment
articles.summary: United States Marines and sailors from the I Marine Expeditionary Force (I MEF) are deploying to the Philippines for the sixth iteration of the Marine Rotational Force-Southeast Asia (MRF-SEA).

blocks.text: November 2, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — United States Marines and sailors from the I Marine Expeditionary Force (I MEF) are deploying to the Philippines for the sixth iteration of the Marine Rotational Force-Southeast Asia (MRF-SEA).
The US Pacific Command said each rotation builds on the relationships and lessons of the force before it, an approach MRF-SEA calls “presence with purpose.”

The US Pacific Command said the deployment marks the second MRF-SEA rotation, building on months of bilateral training and integration between US and Philippine forces, focused on the Philippines to continue a persistent rotational Marine Corps presence designed to strengthen combined readiness and the alliance.

Operating at the invitation of the Philippine government, MRF-SEA serves as I MEF’s forward command element in the Philippines. Marines and sailors work alongside the Armed Forces of the Philippines and Philippine Marine Corps while providing command and control for Marine Corps forces training throughout the archipelago.
“Our goal was never simply to be present in the Philippines,” said Col. Robert Bunn, commanding officer of the outgoing MRF-SEA rotation.

“Presence has to have purpose. Every exercise, planning session and repetition alongside our Philippine Allies was an opportunity to become more interoperable, responsive and capable together, progressively getting better with each event,” Bunn said.
He added the next rotation now has the opportunity to take those lessons and relationships to move the alliance another step forward.
The incoming rotation will continue that progression through the Archipelagic Coastal Defense Continuum and Exercise Balikatan 27.

MANILA, Philippines — The National Food Authority (NFA) has substantially reduced palay handling time and costs in a pilot test of one-ton bags, replacing conventional 50-kilogram sacks in a system that could speed up grain procurement, maximize warehouse capacity, and free up funds for buying more palay.

“Our pilot test showed a 75 percent reduction in handling time and a 50 percent cut in handling costs. Work that used to take an hour can now be completed in just 15 minutes, while handling costs are halved. Using tonner bags also allows us to make better use of warehouse space,” NFA Administrator Larry Lacson said.

Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel Jr., who chairs the NFA Council, said the potential savings could ultimately benefit rice farmers by allowing the agency to stretch its procurement budget and buy more palay from local producers.
Lacson inspected the system at the agency’s Triplex Warehouse in Davao del Sur on Thursday to assess its performance and identify improvements in palay procurement and storage.

articles.title: Big Jim MacLellan, 92, remembered as six-decade pillar of Men of the Deeps
articles.summary: Big Jim MacLellan, from Glace Bay, N.S., was a coal-miner-turned-mine manager best known for his six-decade involvement with The Men of the Deeps choir. The 92-year-old died Friday and is being…

image.caption: James (Big Jim) MacLellan, a longtime Men of the Deeps member, died Friday. (The Men of the Deeps)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia

Big Jim MacLellan, from Glace Bay, N.S., was a coal-miner-turned-mine manager best known for his six-decade involvement with The Men of the Deeps choir. The 92-year-old died Friday and is being remembered for the monologues he delivered about the lives of Cape Breton miners and their communities.
MacLellan retired from the group this year, but continued to play shows with them as recently as September
On his first day of working in a coal mine, 17-year-old James (Big Jim) MacLellan faced an obstacle.
Given MacLellan's six-foot-five-inch frame, his supervisor made an observation.
"The first thing we have to figure out is how the hell we're going to get you in there," the supervisor said.
MacLellan, from Glace Bay, N.S., was a coal-miner-turned-mine manager best known for his six-decade involvement with The Men of the Deeps, the famed men's chorus made up of miners.
MacLellan's height made him stand out on stage, but it was the monologues he delivered talking about the lives of coal miners and their communities that people remembered.

"Everybody in the audience was either crying from laughing so hard or crying from being emotional because he had an excellent way of crafting the whole thing," said Jenn Sheppard, who is writing a book about the group's history.
MacLellan, 92, died Friday.

He was a founding member of the group, and although he officially retired from The Men of the Deeps earlier this year, he was still performing shows with them as late as September. He was the last original member to perform with the group, but is not the last surviving original member.
MacLellan, centre, is shown in a photo from his early days with The Men of the Deeps. (CBC)

"He loved it. He loved the camaraderie, spending time with the guys and interacting with the audience … it meant a lot to him," said Jim MacLellan, one of MacLellan's six children. He said he was known as Little Jim because he was only six-foot-two.

While being a member of The Men of the Deeps took MacLellan across Canada and to parts of the U.S. for shows, his son thinks the joy he derived was equally from the messages he shared about the lives of coal miners.

These included the dangers of the occupation, the teamwork needed to carry out the work, as well as the partnerships on the domestic front where the men worked underground while their spouses managed the lives of the families above ground.
"I think that was the enduring part of being part of the group, was to spread that word and to keep that alive across the country," said Jim MacLellan.
Growing up, he remembers his father rehearsing at home for shows.
MacLellan is shown giving one of his famous monologues during a 2025 show. (CBC)

"We often tormented him that, you know, he would practise singing at home on Sunday afternoon before going to the concert and all the windows were open … as kids of seven, eight years old, we were thoroughly embarrassed," he said.
"You know, your father singing, big baritone voice, belting out the window in the kitchen, right."
While MacLellan joined the group in 1966, he took about a decade off in the mid-1970s to mid-1980s because of his work as a mine manager.
When MacLellan died Friday, The Men of the Deeps was playing a show.
"The fellas were all singing at that same time that Jim passed away and it just seems a bit surreal that it went down that way, but I guess it was meant to be," said choir director Stephen Muise.
60th anniversary

The timing was made all the more remarkable by the fact The Men of the Deeps is performing Sunday in Glace Bay. Today's date marks 60 years to the day of the group's first show — and it's even at the same venue, the Savoy Theatre.
Sheppard said she spent hours interviewing MacLellan about the group's history.

"I think of all the access that he gave us to some ghosts from the past," she said. "You know, we have connections with The Men of the Deeps for years now. And a lot of those guys are gone. And Jim was our last link to a lot of them."
'As sharp as ever'
Even in his later years with the group, MacLellan still performed the monologues.
"He was as sharp as ever," said Muise. "He would tell his stories. He probably had about 100 coal mining stories in his brain and could recount them whenever you needed them."
There are many recordings of shows by The Men of the Deeps. Included on them are MacLellan's monologues, so his legacy lives on.
"Even though we don’t have Jim anymore, we've got those stories," said Muise. "We got them recorded and people can listen to Jim’s stories forever."

articles.title: Some cemeteries flooded during Undas 2026
articles.summary: Some cemeteries in Bulacan and Pampanga failed to escape the brunt of flooding, as parts of their grounds remain submerged during Undas this year.

blocks.text: Published November 1, 2026 11:51pm

Some cemeteries in Bulacan and Pampanga failed to escape the brunt of flooding, as parts of their grounds remain submerged during Undas this year, forcing visitors to climb over walls, tread on tombs, and wear waders to protect themselves from floodwaters.

In a 24 Oras Weekend report by Bea Pinlac on Sunday, although floodwaters had receded in parts of a cemetery in Barangay Masantol, Pampanga—leaving behind moss and mud—several areas remained underwater.
Rogelio was among the visitors forced to step on elevated tombs just to reach his wife’s resting place. However, he decided to light candles for her at home instead.
“Sa bahay na lang, hanggang dito yung tubig eh. Kung lulusong ako baka—may sugat ako eh, hindi pwede sa ‘kin,” Rogelio said.
(I'll just light candles at home because the water reaches up to here. If I wade through it—I have an open wound, so I can't risk it.)
In the report, other visitors laid out sandbags or used ladders to avoid stepping directly into the floodwater.
According to Erwin, another visitor, the flooding had eased compared to last year, allowing his family to finally visit their five departed loved ones who share a single tomb.
“Siyempre masakit. Pag undas lang po doon ka lang po makakapunta tapos baha pa po,” Erwin said.
(Of course it hurts. Undas is the only time you get to visit, and yet it's still flooded.)
Erwin said they plan to elevate the grave of their deceased family members, as it is now gradually sinking into the ground softened by the prolonged flooding.
In preparation for this year’s Undas, local authorities said they installed a protective dike and pumped out water.

“Naglagay po kami ng protection dike para mapalibutan po ‘yung kung saan dumadaan yung tubig, lalo na po kapag nagha-high tide. Ngayon po, humupa na yung tubig. Nag-pump po tayo ng tubig para mailabas po ‘yung tubig sa sementeryo po,” an authority said.
(We put up a protection dike to enclose the pathways where water flows in, especially during high tide. The water has subsided now, and we ran pumps to drain the remaining water out of the cemetery.)
The local government unit plans to reach out to the national government to find a permanent solution to the flooding problem in Barangay Masantol.
Meanwhile, visitor turnout was low for this year’s Undas at inundated cemeteries in Hagonoy, Bulacan.
In a 24 Oras Weekend report by Jaime Santos, floodwaters reached waist- and thigh-deep levels across parts of the Hagonoy Memorial Park in Barangay Sto. Niño.
Residents reported that some remains had already been relocated elsewhere, while relatives of those remaining chose to light candles outside the cemetery grounds instead.

As in Pampanga, visitors at the Peralta Public Cemetery in Barangay San Sebastian faced difficult conditions. Some had to climb over walls, step on tombs, or wear chest waders to protect themselves from health risks posed by the floodwaters.
“Kahit po ganito pa rin ang sitwasyon, wala pa ring pagbabago last year, mahirap baka madulas,” a visitor shared.
(Even though the situation remains the same with no changes since last year, it's still difficult because you could slip.)
“Kailangan pa namin tumalon-talon sa mga nitso para lang makapunta. ‘Yung tatay ko matampuhin ‘yan, kapag ‘di namin nadalaw baka kami ‘yung dalawin sa bahay eh,” another visitor added.
(We had to jump from tomb to tomb just to get through. My father had a short temper—if we don't visit him, he might visit us at home instead.) — Lyjah Tiffany Bonzo/BM, GMA News

articles.title: Tusk defends overhaul of Poland’s constitutional court despite protests
articles.summary:
Prime minister says shake-up is vital to restore tribunal crippled by years of political disputes

Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, has vowed to see through a contested overhaul of the…

blocks.text: Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, has vowed to see through a contested overhaul of the country’s constitutional court, declaring that “in certain matters, there can be no compromise”.

In a prime-time television address on Saturday night, Tusk was defiant, despite overnight protests that saw riot police drafted to protect the court’s building, saying the shake-up was vital to restore a tribunal crippled by years of political disputes.
Paralysed for more than a decade, the court sat at the core of rule of law clashes between the rightwing Law and Justice (PiS) party and the EU during the party’s eight-year rule.

Since returning to office in 2023, the centre-right Tusk has sought to unwind those judicial changes, but his agenda has been frustrated by opposition-aligned presidents with extensive veto powers. Earlier this year, president Karol Nawrocki refused to swear in five judges approved by parliament.

The crisis flared again on Friday when a group of government-backed judges attempted to seize procedural control of the tribunal, suspending the PiS-appointed chief judge and deputy and prompting street protests.

blocks.caption: Conservative supporters assemble outside the constitutional court in Warsaw. Photograph: Agata Grzybowska/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: Defending the action, Tusk said “there was never any doubt that the court in the form imposed by PiS was not a genuine court”, citing adverse rulings from European tribunals.
He compared the opposition outrage to “a thief snatching an elderly woman’s handbag, running off, and when he is caught, he screams that he is subjected to violence”.

Tusk said: “Let’s call things for what they are: for years, there have been organisations and politicians in Poland who seek to destroy democracy and the rule of law. It is no coincidence they find support among pro-Russian forces globally.”

He later highlighted that Russia’s former president Dmitry Medvedev had joined the opposition in an outcry over the changes, accusing Warsaw of “a constitutional coup” and “hounding the conservatives”. “And everything is clear,” Tusk said.

He also criticised opposition-aligned Nawrocki for joining the protests on Friday night and forcing his entry into the court’s building to intervene. “In a democratic state, no politician can enter a court to issue orders or intimidate judges – not even the president,” Tusk said. “We Poles have succeeded too well in building a strong state to surrender now.”
He said it was the government’s duty to ensure its security and the conditions necessary for the court to operate. “And I intend to fulfil that duty,” he said.
On Saturday, the European Commission urged Nawrocki to approve the new judges who were nominated by parliament, so the court could function in line with the constitution and EU law.
A spokesperson for the commission said its executive was “following closely” the events in Poland.
after newsletter promotion

“It is for the Polish authorities to ensure that the constitutional tribunal can function in accordance with the Polish constitution and in respect of the relevant case law of the court of justice of the European Union,” the spokesperson said, appearing to ally the bloc with the Polish government.

However, the spokesperson also highlighted that the European court of human rights issued an interim finding in May that obliged Polish authorities to “refrain from hindering the taking up and exercise of judicial duties” by judges who are still waiting to be sworn in.
The confrontation sets the battle lines before next year’s parliamentary election, with polls pointing to a close race between Tusk’s broad coalition and the nationalist right.
However, experts remain divided over whether the government’s procedural gambit at the court is lawful.
Poland’s Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights said on Saturday the legal basis for the temporary suspension was “questionable”, warning it would “not contribute” to restoring the court.

The foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, conceded that the events outside the court were “not elegant”, but insisted: “The alternative was to concede an unconstitutional transformation of Poland into a presidential republic.”

Nawrocki held some cross-party political talks on Saturday, with no apparent breakthrough. His senior aide, Zbigniew Bogucki, responded to Tusk’s address, calling the prime minister “a pathological liar, who is setting Poland ablaze”.

articles.title: Republican senator Dan Sullivan says he will accept Alaska election results
articles.summary:
Senator was allegedly targeted in ballot-stacking ploy by his Democratic opponent to peel away votes from him

Senator Dan Sullivan, the Alaska Republican allegedly targeted in a…

blocks.text: Senator Dan Sullivan, the Alaska Republican allegedly targeted in a ballot-stacking ploy by his Democratic opponent, Mary Peltola, told CNN this morning that he would accept the results of his upcoming election.

According to a recent New York Times investigation, aides from Peltola’s campaign recruited another man who shared Sullivan’s name to join the race in a ploy to peel away votes from the Republican incumbent.

Since those revelations, Republicans, including Donald Trump, have called for Peltola to be disqualified from the race and criminally prosecuted. Peltola has continued to deny any knowledge of such a scheme on the part of her campaign, recently telling a reporter at a campaign event that she had “no idea” if any of her staff were involved.
Asked by CNN’s Jake Tapper if he would only accept the election results if he won, Sullivan responded: “No, I’m going to accept the election results.”

Earlier in his interview with Tapper, Sullivan also said he wasn’t focused on how Peltola’s campaign might be legally challenged. He was focused instead on winning the race outright. He nonetheless expressed doubt that Peltola had lacked any knowledge of the effort to put a second Dan Sullivan on the ballot.
“She’s continually lying to the Alaskan people,” Sullivan said. “And I guarantee you, she’s lying right now.”

Meanwhile, the Washington Post reported that Republicans tried to boost unviable Democratic candidates in the Alaska primaries as well. A Republican Super Pac boosted two candidates for Senate who did not live in Alaska, and praised them as “progressives” similar to Bernie Sanders.

items: Philip Ella 'Popoy' Juico, former chairman of the Philippine Sports Commission, passed away on October 31 at the age of 78 after battling cancer since 2022.

Juico served as the PSC chair from 1996 to 1998 and held various leadership roles in local sports, including president of the Philippine Athletics Track and Field Association and involvement in volleyball leagues.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – Former Philippine Sports Commission (PSC) chairman Philip Ella “Popoy” Juico died on Saturday, October 31, his family announced. He was 78.

“After courageously battling cancer since 2022, my Papa passed away peacefully in his sleep. While our hearts are filled with sadness, we find comfort in knowing that he is finally free from pain and suffering and is now resting in God’s loving embrace,” his son Joseph Juico, a councilor for the 1st District of Quezon City, said in a social media post on Sunday, November 1.
Vincent Juico also announced on Sunday his father’s passing, thanking the public for the “prayers and understanding.”
The elder Juico served as the country’s sports chief from 1996 to 1998 under Philippine president Fidel V. Ramos, who appointed the longtime public servant as the fourth PSC chair.
He held various leadership roles in local sports, including as president of the Philippine Athletics Track and Field Association (PATAFA) from 2015 to 2022.
Juico also became active in volleyball, helping form the Philippine Super Liga in 2013 and the Shakey’s Super League in 2022.
On the international front, Juico acted as vice president and chair of the School and Youth Commission of the Asian Athletics Association from 2015 to 2019.
But before his foray into sports, Juico served as secretary of the Department of Agrarian Reform from 1987 to 1989 under president Corazon Aquino.

In 1987, he was honored as one of the Ten Outstanding Young Men for government service. He was also recognized by his alma mater, De La Salle University, which inducted him into its Sports Hall of Fame in 2001 for his contributions to Philippine sports.
The wake and memorial services will be held from November 4 to 5 at the Santuario de San Antonio in Forbes Park, Makati City. Inurnment will follow on November 6.
Juico is survived by his wife, former Philippine Charity Sweepstakes Office chair Margie Penson-Juico, and children Dinggay, Vincent, Joseph, and Mayen. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Crash that killed 4 teens in Puslinch, Ont., an 'unimaginable tragedy': police
articles.summary: Four teens, aged 15 to 19 years, died in a crash in Puslinch, a rural area southeast of Guelph, early Saturday, according to Ontario Provincial Police.

image.caption: A crash that killed four young people in Puslinch early Saturday was an 'unimaginable tragedy', according to Ontario Provincial Police. (CBC)

blocks.text: Kitchener-Waterloo
Four teens, aged 15 to 19 years, died in a crash in Puslinch, a rural area southeast of Guelph, early Saturday, according to Ontario Provincial Police.
2 of 6 passengers recovering in hospital from single-vehicle crash Saturday, police say
A single-vehicle crash that killed four teens, aged 15 to 19, in Puslinch early Saturday was an "unimaginable tragedy," according to Ontario Provincial Police.

The dead included a 19-year-old man from Mississauga, a 19-year-old man from Brampton, a 17-year-old girl Mississauga and a 15-year-old girl from Milton, OPP Insp. Karen Madeiros said at a press conference Sunday.
"This is a devastating event that has impacted multiple families schools friend groups and communities across southern Ontario," said Madeiros.
A 17-year-old girl with life-altering injuries and a 16-year-old girl with non-life-threatening injuries remain in hospital, Madeiros said.

Officers were called to a rural area southeast of Guelph shortly after 1:30 a.m. Saturday. In the area of Watson Road S. and Wellington Road 34, a vehicle had left the road, struck a guardrail and fallen into a ravine, Madeiros said.
Roads were closed in the area on Saturday as investigators were at the scene of the crash, the OPP said. (Andrew Collins/CBC)
"Four young people have lost their lives in a matter of moments. Families have been forever changed and an entire community is searching for answers," she said.
She urged anyone with information or footage to contact the Wellington County OPP.
Details that might seem insignificant could actually be valuable to investigators piecing together the circumstances of this tragedy, Madeiros said.
Complex investigation ongoing: OPP inspector
Superint. Wendy Burrow expressed her condolences on behalf of the OPP for the lives lost in the crash, calling it an "unimaginable tragedy that claimed the lives of four young people."
"These young people will never have the opportunity to realize their hopes, dreams and aspirations that they envisioned for their futures," she said.
The OPP is supporting those affected by the crash and will ensure "every effort is made" to provide loved ones with answers on what happened, Burrow said.

The complex investigation is ongoing and officers are looking to determine what happened in the moments leading up to the crash, Madeiros said. Investigators will look at whether speed and seatbelt use were factors, she said.
"Our responsibility is to ensure those answers are based on evidence, facts and a thorough investigation," Madeiros said.

articles.title: Tributes paid to ‘inspiring’ Cambridge scientist who died in Spain train crash
articles.summary:
Dr Marta Shahbazi was travelling to a conference to receive award for scientific excellence in developmental biology

An “inspiring” University of Cambridge scientist died in the

blocks.text: An “inspiring” University of Cambridge scientist died in the Spanish train collision on Wednesday that killed at least 69 people.

Dr Marta Shahbazi, an affiliate associate professor at the Cambridge Stem Cell Institute and a group leader at the city’s Medical Research Council Laboratory of Molecular Biology (LMB), was travelling on one of the trains involved in the crash near Urda in Toledo province.

The LMB said the mother of two had recently won the Spanish Society of Developmental Biology’s scientific excellence prize. She had been due to be presented with the award during its conference in El Rompido, Andalucía.

In a LinkedIn post, the LMB said it was deeply saddened by her death, which was “a profound shock and a huge loss”, adding: “Martha was an inspiring, talented and passionate scientist whose research shed light on the earliest steps in the development of human embryos and how errors occur that lead to failed pregnancies.”
It said she was a role model who had written eloquently about balancing her family and career, describing herself as a “mother scientist”.

Dr Roser Vento-Tormo, a group leader at the Wellcome Sanger Institute outside Cambridge, wrote: “Marta Shahbazi was a beautiful person: a close collaborator, a treasured friend, and an inspiration to me both as a scientist and as a mother.

“As a scientist, we shared so many dreams. We co-supervised two students together, and I cannot describe how much joy it was to work alongside her. Some of our work will still be published in the coming months, and anyone who reads it will feel the passion she poured into everything she did …
“My thoughts are with her family. Anyone who knew Marta could see how deeply they were a unit, and how much they meant to her.”
The Center for Research in Molecular Medicine and Chronic Diseases (CiMUS), based in Santiago de Compostela, Spain, paid tribute to Shahbazi as “a brilliant young researcher”.

The disaster was Spain’s second high-speed rail crash this year. Both collisions occurred on the line between the central city of Madrid, Spain’s capital, and Seville, in the Andalucía region in the south of the country.
Three days of national mourning were observed from Thursday. The Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, described the incident as a “tragedy” and has promised an investigation.

articles.title: Proposed data centre would release ‘23 Hiroshima-sized atomic bombs worth of energy’ a day, physicist says
articles.summary: An analysis of the mammoth Wonder Valley data centre suggests it would release the equivalent of 23 atom bombs of heat waste into the boreal forest of northwestern Alberta every day. A Utah State…

image.caption: A project map shows the phases of O'Leary Digital's Wonder Valley data centre, which would be located about 42 kilometres south of Grande Prairie in the Municipal District of Greenview. (O'Leary Digital Limited)

blocks.text: Edmonton

An analysis of the mammoth Wonder Valley data centre suggests it would release the equivalent of 23 atom bombs of heat waste into the boreal forest of northwestern Alberta every day. A Utah State University physicist who conducted the review for the Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation said the project demands a full environmental impact assessment.
Northern Alberta First Nation continues to battle Kevin O’Leary-backed project in court

An analysis of the mammoth data centre proposed by celebrity investor Kevin O’Leary suggests it would release the equivalent of 23 atom bombs of heat waste into the boreal forest of northwestern Alberta every day.

If the Wonder Valley project goes ahead, “‘about 23 Hiroshima-sized atomic bombs worth of energy every single day will get dumped into that landscape,” said Utah State University physicist Robert Davies.
“The effect will almost certainly be large, if not extreme,” said Davies, who conducted a preliminary analysis for the Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation (SLCN) earlier this year.
In September, the nation filed for a judicial review of the project’s exemption from a provincial environmental impact assessment.
"I can't imagine allowing it to go forward without those full assessments,” Davies said, describing the project’s potential to be “the largest single-site heat source on the entire planet.”

O’Leary Digital Limited’s $70-billion data centre is proposed for the Municipal District of Greenview, south of Grande Prairie and roughly 130 kilometres southwest of SLCN’s reserve, in the First Nation’s traditional territory.

items: Updated info about water use, timelines for proposed Wonder Valley AI project in Alberta
Northern Albertans raise concerns about Wonder Valley AI data centre at packed community hall
'We have serious concerns,’ northern Alberta chief says after hosting community meeting on Wonder Valley

blocks.text: At full operation, it would release around 18 gigawatts of heat a day and about 30 million tonnes of carbon dioxide a year — more than four per cent of Canada’s total emissions, said Davies, whose assessment was based on publicly available information.
“When people talk about environmental regulations that these projects have to adhere to, those regulations were not created with anything of this scale in mind.”
SLCN filed the judicial review application in September and requested another review in court last month to demand more consultation before the project can go ahead.
Wonder Valley’s unprecedented scale warrants more rigorous discussion, said SLCN’s lawyer, Orlagh O’Kelly.
Province responds to judicial reviews

In a Oct. 30 statement, Alberta’s Ministry of Environment and Protected Areas said it followed the established legal process to determine that no environmental impact assessment (EIA) was required for the project.

EIAs “are typically required when a project, or components of a project, involve technologies or systems with unknown environmental impacts. In this case, the project uses standard, proven power and water systems that have been safely used in Alberta for decades,” the statement said.

“Even when an EIA is not triggered, proponents must still obtain all required permits, provide detailed technical assessments on impacts to air, land, and water, and demonstrate the project can be built and operated safely before any project can proceed.”

items: Will Meta’s data centre raise Alberta power bills? Experts say it could
UCP fall agenda prioritizes 'merit' hiring, data centres, standardizing report cards
Proposed data centre in west-central Alberta prompts pushback from some residents, support from others

blocks.text: The permitting process can’t measure the entire impact of a project, Davies countered.
“Permits check the parts. An assessment checks the whole. A project this size is exactly what assessments are for.”
The Ministry of Indigenous Relations said it is unable to comment on the review regarding consultation, while the matter is before the courts.
Piecemeal litigation
Along with the province, the M.D of Greenview and O’Leary Digital are also named as respondents in SLCN’s filings.

“We also respect the robust and stringent regulatory process we must follow in advancing Wonder Valley,” O’Leary Digital CEO Paul Palandjian wrote in an Oct. 27 email. “Meanwhile, we’re having productive dialogue with Indigenous communities through consultation and engagement, and we remain committed to that work."

Greenview Reeve Ryan Ratzlaff said the district always pursues development in a “responsible, respectful and collaborative manner,” noting that environmental oversight and Indigenous consultation fall under the purview of the Alberta government.

A new sign, installed earlier this year, sits along Highway 40 at the entrance to the Greenview Industrial Gateway which would be the home of Wonder Valley if the project is green-lit. (Eagle Andersen/CBC)

SLCN is also in the midst of another court battle with O’Leary Digital, after a judge dismissed the company’s bid to strike down a judicial review on consultation and water rights, which initially went in the nation’s favour.
O’Kelly said the current system forces First Nations to file legal challenges to be heard, calling it "deliberately bifurcated and piecemeal."
This is the project that went the absolute wrong way.Chief Sheldon Sunshine
Chief Sheldon Sunshine said SLCN has built productive relationships with other oil and gas developers, but the nation’s experience with Wonder Valley has been difficult since it was announced.
“If anybody's to learn anything about this — this is the project that went the absolute wrong way.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Eagle Andersen is a reporter for CBC News in Grande Prairie. He previously worked as an associate producer for CBC News in Kamloops, B.C. You can reach him at eagle.andersen@cbc.ca.

articles.title: France opens attempted murder probe after protest attack
articles.summary: Paris prosecutors have opened an attempted murder investigation after a Molotov attack on police. France reported 779 arrests during nationwide protests and Halloween night, fewer than on previous…

image.caption: Violence broke out during nationwide demonstrations over living costs and inequality in FranceImage: Raphaël Lafargue/abaca/picture alliance

blocks.text: Paris prosecutors opened an attempted murder investigation Sunday after a Molotov cocktail was thrown at security forces during a demonstration in the French capital.

Prosecutors said explosive projectiles targeted about 15 gendarmes as well as police officers. No suspects have been arrested over the attack, and investigators were still establishing the number and severity of injuries.
What happened in Paris?

The attack took place at Porte de Charenton, where Saturday's march ended. Photographs and video from the AFP news agency showed an incendiary device exploding at a gendarme's feet and setting his protective equipment alight.
Prosecutors said reported injuries included second-degree burns and tinnitus, although those details remained provisional. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez described the attack as an attempted murder.
How many people were arrested?

The Interior Ministry reported 779 arrests nationwide during the demonstrations and Halloween night. The figure includes both events, updating Saturday evening's provisional total of 565. Authorities said the later part of the night passed without major incidents.
Paris prosecutors separately reported 105 arrests in the capital: 88 linked to the demonstrations and 17 to Halloween night. They said 89 people remained in custody, including at least 22 minors.

blocks.caption: A protester holds a placard calling for French President Emmanuel Macron to work in a mine and billionaires in factoriesImage: Abdul Saboor/REUTERS

blocks.text: The protests focused on high living costs and government policies. The ministry put nationwide turnout at 320,000, while unions estimated nearly 500,000 participants.

The nationwide arrest total was below the 1,314 recorded during the previous Saturday's mobilization and the 2,628 on October 17, when widespread rioting and looting broke out. Authorities had increased security ahead of Halloween amid online calls for violence.

articles.title: Carney calls December byelections for 6 ridings in Ontario, Quebec and Saskatchewan
articles.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney has called byelections for a total of six ridings located in Saskatchewan, Ontario and Quebec that will give the Liberals a chance to strengthen their thin majority in the…

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney on Parliament Hill on Wednesday. Byelections to fill six vacant seats in the House of Commons will be contested in December, Carney has announced. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

Prime Minister Mark Carney has called byelections for a total of six ridings located in Saskatchewan, Ontario and Quebec that will give the Liberals a chance to strengthen their thin majority in the House of Commons.
Races on Dec. 7 give Liberals a chance to bolster majority in the House of Commons
· CBC News
· Posted: Nov 01, 2026 9:35 AM EST | Last Updated: 23 minutes ago

Prime Minister Mark Carney has called byelections for a total of six ridings located in Ontario, Quebec and Saskatchewan — races that will give the Liberals a chance to strengthen their thin majority in the House of Commons.
The byelections will be held on Dec. 7, according to a news release sent out Sunday morning.

Half of the races will be in Quebec, in the ridings of Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot-Acton, Rosemont-La Petite-Patrie and Laurier-Sainte-Marie — seats previously held by Bloc Québécois, NDP and Liberal MPs, respectively.
In Ontario, the ridings to be contested are Scarborough North and Brantford-Brant South.
Former Liberal MP Shaun Chen, who had held Scarborough North since 2015, stepped down last August citing health issues. He later ran for Toronto City Council and won.
In September, Conservative Larry Brock resigned as MP for Brantford-Brant South. Prior to his resignation, Brock said he had accepted a position at the Brantford Crown Attorney's office.
Liberals flip Quebec riding in byelection sweep, CBC News projects
The Saskatchewan riding is Yorkton-Melville. Conservative Cathay Wagantall had held the seat since 2015 before officially stepping down at the end of August.

As it stands, the Liberals have a thin majority in the House of Commons with 173 seats. Losing all six races will not affect their ability to govern, but wins will allow the party to bolster its ranks.

items: Scott Aitchison’s resignation sets stage for a competitive Parry Sound–Muskoka byelection

blocks.text: Another riding will soon be vacant: Parry Sound–Muskoka, which has been represented by Conservative MP Scott Aitchison since 2019. In September, Aitchison said he would officially step down at the end of the fall sitting.
Who's running in Quebec
In the lead-up to the byelection call, parties have been steadily announcing their candidates.

For the Quebec races, the Liberals are running former Quebec MNA Chantal Soucy in Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot-Acton, human rights advocate Jean-Sébastien Vallée in Rosemont-La Petite-Patrie and former Desjardins CEO Guy Cormier in Laurier-Sainte-Marie.
Former Montreal Alouettes player Luc Brodeur-Jourdain will run under the Conservative banner in Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot-Acton. The party has not yet announced candidates in the other two contests.
Elections Canada signs in the Beaches-East York riding in Toronto on Aug. 31. (Keito Newman/The Canadian Press)

The NDP will run Mathieu Boisvert in Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot, former Parti Québécois leadership candidate and labour advocate Pierre Céré in Rosemont-La Petite-Patrie, and epidemiologist Nimâ Machouf in Laurier-Sainte-Marie.

The Bloc Québécois has confirmed former director general of the International Dairy Federation, Caroline Émond, will run under its banner in Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot-Acton. No other candidates have been announced yet.

In a statement to CBC News on Friday, the Green Party confirmed Martin Grenier will run in Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot-Acton, while nominations remain open in Rosemont-La Petite-Patrie and Laurier-Sainte-Marie.
Candidates in Ontario and Saskatchewan

In Scarborough North, the Liberals are running former Toronto District School Board trustee James Li and the Greens are running Vicki Jewt. The Conservatives and NDP have not yet announced their candidates.
For Brantford-Brant South, the Liberals will run Joy O'Donnell, president of the Chamber of Commerce Brantford-Brant. The Conservatives will run Brantford Mayor Kevin Davis.
The NDP has not yet announced its candidate, and the Green Party says nominations are open in that riding as well.
Larry Brock stepped down as MP for the Ontario riding Brantford–Brant South, formerly Brantford–Brant South–Six Nations, in September. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

The Conservatives may face a challenge in Brantford-Brant South after the party chose to bypass a local nomination contest and appoint Davis as its candidate. The party said at the time it wanted to ensure a candidate was ready to hit the ground running.

After the appointment of Davis as candidate, pastor and longtime Conservative Dave Carroll announced he would run as an independent candidate in the riding. That could draw votes away from Davis, who is already expected to face an uphill battle against the Liberals.
In Yorkton-Melville, the Liberals are running Aaron Kienle, the Conservatives are running Nelson Pohl and the Greens will run Valerie Brooks. The NDP has not confirmed its candidate yet.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Benjamin Lopez Steven is an associate producer for CBC's The House and a digital writer with CBC Politics. He was also a 2024 Joan Donaldson Scholar and a graduate of Carleton University. You can reach him at benjamin.steven@cbc.ca or find him on X at @bensteven_s.

The Ukrainian military evacuated a further 167 civilians from the partially occupied southern region of Kherson on Sunday, the army's general staff confirmed shortly before a localized six-day ceasefire was due to expire.
Among the evacuees were 22 children and 21 people with limited mobility, according to the announcement.
The temporary truce in and around the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky is set to expire at 11 p.m. local time (10 p.m. CET).
Local governor Olexander Prokudin called on residents in the region to remain alert and warned people not to enter or approach areas close to the Dnipro river which flows through Kherson.
