articles.title: [Inside the Newsroom] The DICT circus, Almirol’s suspension, and our tech coverage refocus
articles.summary: We are living in a world where technology is no longer optional. It has invaded our homes and each of our personal spaces.

blocks.text: We are living in a world where technology is no longer optional. It has invaded our homes and each of our personal spaces.

On October 21, the Office of the Ombudsman ordered a six-month preventive suspension without pay against Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) Undersecretary David Almirol Jr.

It cited findings of conflict of interest: the eGov project, which Almirol led, awarded contracts worth P1.55 billion to a company that eventually subcontracted work to Multisys Technologies Corporation, a company he founded.
The suspension order came almost a year after Rappler exposed the issue in an investigative report published in December 2025.

The report was triggered by a DICT internal audit report that Rappler got hold of. To get to the bottom of the issue, we spent months scouring through corporate information and financial disclosures submitted by Multisys to the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) as well as DICT procurement records. We interviewed numerous sources, including Almirol himself.
Hello! I am Gemma Mendoza, head for strategic programs and one of the geeks minding our technology coverage here at Rappler.
Apart from this story, we have also been closely monitoring the circus at the DICT, including:

items: the clumsy effort to go after Discord and platforms used by nihilist violent extremists to prey on kids;
the exit of DICT Secretary Henry Aguda; and
the appointment of the former Social Security System chief Robert Joseph de Claro.

blocks.text: This is part of an effort in Rappler to cover technology and platforms from the perspective of public welfare, rights, safety, and accountability.

To maximize our energies, we do less reviews of the latest gadgets and gizmos and do more stories that help the public understand how innovations and developments in technology — and how the policies and actions of governments, including our own government, in relation to this sector — could affect their lives.

For instance, an investigative report we recently published uncovered how a sprawling online community of 430,000 members abuses women by gamifying the non-consensual disclosure of their intimate moments. The report also exposed gaps in laws that allow such platforms to flourish.

We will continue scrutinizing developments in Silicon Valley and the giant companies behind these technologies. But we will be looking at these from the perspective of citizens from the global majority whose voices and perspectives are often taken as an afterthought in a world dominated by the tech titans.

We feel this is critical because digital technologies have become so pervasive that it is virtually impossible for the ordinary individual to evade them. From the moment we wake up in the morning to when we go to sleep — and even as we sleep — we take these technologies with us.
In workshops we conduct across the country, I often joke that our phones and the digital platforms we use know more about us than the people closest to us.
This is the reason our newsroom’s technology and platforms cluster decided to revive our #EverydayTech chat room in the Muni tab of Rappler’s app.
We realized that while technologies and platforms are so much a part of our lives, very few people really understand how they work.

For instance, Digital 2027, the latest report by creative marketing agency We Are Social, shows that 3.24 billion individuals or nearly 40% of the global population already use generative AI tools each month.

However, few people realize that, beyond the seeming magic, generative AI is basically a tool that processes huge amounts of data scraped — often without permission — from various websites all over the internet.
Few also realize that when they talk to that friendly chatbot, they are in fact potentially giving away precious sensitive personal information which could be abused and used against them.
These are among the things we discuss daily, at 10 am and 4 pm in the #EverydayTech chat room.
You might ask, what does this have to do with the story on Almirol and the DICT?

Simple: the DICT is primarily responsible for promoting the Philippine government’s national information and communications technology (ICT) development agenda. It is supposed to ensure that Filipinos benefit from emerging technologies while also ensuring that our people are not being harmed by such technologies.

Our coverage intends to not just scrutinize how the technology platforms are behaving and operating, but also how various responsible agencies of government tasked to protect our interests are responding to such developments.
We invite you to collaborate with us in this journey.
Jump in whenever you can and join the conversation in the #EverydayTech channel. Do invite others to join as well.
And if you have leads on stories involving platforms and government agencies that are supposed to be regulating them, send us tips through investigative@rappler.com.
If you have the wherewithal, do support our investigations by joining Rappler+ or by giving whatever you can to our crowdfunding effort.

We are living in a world where technology is no longer optional. It has invaded our homes and each of our personal spaces. Let us explore, understand, and investigate how it affects us together. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Don't like daylight saving time? Nova Scotia once lost 11 days in a single night
articles.summary: People in the entire British Empire went to bed on Sept. 2, 1752, and woke up on Sept. 14, 1752.

image.caption: The next edition of the weekly Halifax Gazette after Aug. 29 was issued on the new date of Sept. 16 rather than Sept. 5. (Nova Scotia Archives)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia
People in the entire British Empire went to bed on Sept. 2, 1752, and woke up on Sept. 14, 1752.
A switch from the Julian to Gregorian calendar in 1752 wiped away more than a week across the British Empire
Spring forward, fall back.
Twice a year, much of the country issues a collective grumble when the time comes to adjust the clocks.
That modern hassle pales in comparison to 1752, when 11 days vanished into thin air.
People in the entire British Empire went to bed on Sept. 2 and woke up, presumably refreshed and a bit peckish, on Sept. 14.

In 1750, the British Parliament passed "An Act for regulating the Commencement of the Year, and for correcting the Calendar now in use," titled the Calendar (New Style) Act 1750. The legislation was set to take effect two years later.
Halifax had been founded three years before the date change. (Thomas Jefferys/Archives of Nova Scotia)
For many, it was an overdue change. At the time Britain was still using the Julian calendar, while most of Western Europe had adopted the Gregorian calendar introduced by Pope Gregory XIII in 1582.

As historian Robin Eagles notes on The History of Parliament website, by 1752 "Britain was out of step with the continent by eleven days." The discrepancy was "further complicated by the use of 25 March rather than 1 January in England as the beginning of the year."
Under the provisions of the act, the 11 days were dropped after Sept. 2, 1752. The next day became Sept. 14.

The shift was especially confusing in the Maritimes, where the Acadians had already been using the Gregorian calendar for generations. The French had adopted the calendar in December 1582, so when the British in Nova Scotia made the switch in 1752, they were simply catching up to a system the French-speaking population already followed.
Gov. Edward Cornwallis and the Acadians were at loggerheads at the time of the calendar change. (Sir Joshua Reynolds/Art Gallery of Nova Scotia)

The Acadians likely spent little time dwelling on the shift. They were already locked in a confrontation with Gov. Edward Cornwallis over their refusal to swear an unconditional oath of allegiance to the British Crown — a standoff that culminated in their forced expulsion just three years later.
To alleviate concerns across the empire, the British government explicitly declared that removing the 11 days did not allow anyone to collect rent or interest early.
Despite accounts of widespread "calendar riots" in England with people demanding their 11 days back, most historians regard this as an urban myth.
The first edition of the Halifax Gazette in March 1752 noted the upcoming change in passing, but never followed up on it. (Nova Scotia Archives)
The calendar change is reflected in a date jump in periodicals and colonial records, but otherwise caused no widespread disruption.
But further adjustments may be needed in the long run. At the time, Benjamin Franklin noted in Poor Richard's Almanack that even the Gregorian calendar would need fine tuning eventually.
"Here is still an Excess of one Hour, twenty Minutes, in four Centuries; which in 72 Centuries will amount to a whole Day."

image.caption: Kenny Jacquard of Lobster Fishing Areas 33 and 34 said the rising fuel costs will drive more harvesters to inshore fishing and intensify competition. (Submitted by Kenny Jacquard)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia
As the season opening looms for southwestern Nova Scotia's lobster zone, fishermen face mounting uncertainty from skyrocketing fuel prices among other concerns.
Harvesters say rising costs mean they’ll need a high price to have a profitable season.
Lobster fishermen in southwestern Nova Scotia are feeling the squeeze from soaring fuel prices.

In an interview with CBC's Information Morning Nova Scotia on Thursday, two guests from Lobster Fishing Areas (LFAs) 33 and 34 — one a commercial harvester — said high diesel costs will likely force vessels to make fewer trips and stay closer to shore.

Kenny Jacquard, a veteran fisherman from Wedgeport, N.S., with more than 30 years of experience, said this shift could strain inshore waters and increase competition among crews, as larger boats that normally fish further offshore stay closer to land to save fuel.
"It's going to put so much more lobster traps in the inshore that it's going to clean out all the lobsters probably before Christmas," Jacquard said.
As of Friday, the minimum price for diesel stands at $2.66 per litre, according to the Nova Scotia Energy Board.

LFAs 33 and 34 are scheduled to open for harvesting on Nov. 30. Donnie Jacquard, who is closely involved with the fishery, said he has heard "horror stories" about fuel costs from those who harvest groundfish.

"Right now, the price of diesel fuel is going to force a lot of the lobster fishermen to go out less, instead of going out, let's say four times a week," he said. "So it's going to hurt everybody in the long run."

items: ‘A kick in the butt’: N.S. farmers struggle with wet hay, high fuel prices
N.S. volunteer fire departments sound alarm over fuel costs

blocks.text: Both noted that high fuel costs drive up the price of nearly everything else, from fishing gear to daily living costs. Those expenses, they warned, will eventually be passed along to the market rate.
Kenny Jacquard said that lobster prices would need to reach almost $20 a pound for operations to remain profitable, though trade tariffs and market conditions add uncertainty.

He said he believes a lot of people are worried. "Not everybody will have a bad year because there's always boats that will do OK, but for the majority, I would say people won't be in as good shape as they usually are."
The region's lobster industry faces broader pressures beyond fuel prices.

Dan Fleck, executive director of the Brazil Rock 33/34 Lobster Association, said catches in LFA 34 have dropped 50 per cent over the past decade, similar to trends in the Bay of Fundy, for reasons that remain unknown.
While LFA 33 harvest numbers have remained stable, Fleck said southwestern Nova Scotia remains vulnerable because of its heavy reliance on the lobster fishery.
"In other parts of the Maritimes, they have other fisheries they can rely upon — tuna, snow crab, shrimp, halibut," Fleck said, but in southwestern Nova Scotia "lobster is it."
Despite the uncertainties leading into opening day, Fleck said harvesters still hope for a bountiful season and a decent price.

articles.title: Explainer: How could Israel break the election deadlock?
articles.summary: Israel's election leaves no clear path to forming a government, with Benjamin Netanyahu facing an opposition majority. Here are four possible scenarios that could determine the country's political…

blocks.text: A woman passes by a banner depicting Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and US President Donald Trump day after the country held a national election, in Jerusalem, on October 28 , 2026.
Ronen Zvulun/Reuters

Israel's election leaves no clear path to forming a government, with Benjamin Netanyahu facing an opposition majority. Here are four possible scenarios that could determine the country's political future.

items: Israel's recent election resulted in no clear winner, leaving Benjamin Netanyahu as caretaker prime minister while facing an opposition majority in parliament.
Potential scenarios include another election if no candidate can form a government, or a unity government that may require Netanyahu to abandon his far-right allies.
Eisenkot could attempt to form a minority government with support from Arab parties, but this may be challenging due to public sentiment against Arab political involvement.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

JERUSALEM – Israel’s election this week was indecisive and there is no clear winner poised to form a government. Benjamin Netanyahu remains in office as caretaker prime minister, but faces a parliament stacked with an opposition majority vying to oust him.
Here are some scenarios that could follow:

After the formal final election results are published next week, Israel’s President Isaac Herzog begins consultations with party representatives and then taps the candidate whom he deems to have the best chance to form a government.

If the candidate fails, another can try and if that candidate fails, the Knesset can nominate another. There is a deadline for the process of around 100 days. If no one succeeds, another election is held.
Herzog said on Wednesday that everything must be done to avoid another election and urged the parties to come with an open mind to the consultations with him.

Netanyahu’s Likud party, emerging as the largest in the Knesset, forms a coalition that would likely include centrist and right-wing opposition parties such as Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar, the second-largest party, Avigdor Lieberman’s Israel Our Home and Naftali Bennett’s Together faction.
That grouping would secure 66 seats, a majority in the 120-seat parliament.

However, this option appears remote at this point because it would mean Netanyahu would likely have to abandon his natural political allies, the far-right and ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties. Further, the opposition parties would have to break their main election pledge to their voters: unseating Netanyahu.
Still, if neither camp is able to form a government at the end of weeks of protracted negotiations, a unity government may emerge as a last option.
Renewed fighting with Iran, or other players, could also push the sides together.

If Herzog taps Eisenkot first, he could try to form a government with Yashar’s natural allies — Together, The Democrats and Israel Our Home — propped up by Israel’s two Arab parties, even if they are not members of this government: Ra’am and the Joint List.
Eisenkot’s camp would number 48 seats, according to the latest vote tally, with the Arab parties numbering 19 seats that together reach a 67-seat majority.

But even if Eisenkot reverses his campaign pledge not to have Arab parties in government and accepts their support, it would be a hard sell to many Israelis whose attitudes toward Israel’s Arab minority have hardened further since the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack.

Netanyahu has focused his campaign on delegitimizing support from Arab parties, who surged to record heights in Tuesday’s election, and for now, only The Democrats, a centre-left party, has come out publicly calling for their inclusion.
Both Arab parties have signalled that they are prepared to cooperate with Eisenkot’s camp.
Ra’am joined Bennett’s government ​in 2021, the first time an independent Arab party entered an Israeli coalition. That government collapsed after 18 months.

Netanyahu’s coalition has fallen from its original 64 seats to 53, according to the latest election results. But Israel’s longest-serving leader is viewed as one of its most skilled politicians and he could split the opposition by peeling away members of its parties and bringing them over to his side.

He has managed to do this before, including as opposition head in the run-up to the 2022 election, which he won. But the coalition he was battling at the time had a far narrower lead and he did not need too many defectors to destabilize his political rivals. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Why musicians are touring less and expecting fans to come to them
articles.summary: Attending a concert is no longer just a night out: with the rise of the music residency and select-city tours, artists are saving on travel costs, while fans have to shell out for what's being sold…

image.caption: The Backstreet Boys perform onstage at Little Caesars Arena in Detroit, Michigan, in December 2022. They're currently doing a musical residency in Vegas, attracting millions of fans over their run. And in Toronto, they're hosting a 12-night residency in Toronto. (Scott Legato/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Cost of Living·New

Attending a concert is no longer just a night out: with the rise of the music residency and select-city tours, artists are saving on travel costs, while fans have to shell out for what's being sold being as the trip of a lifetime.
Streaming has cut into artists' income, so there's more pressure for live shows
First, comes the concert tickets.
Then the flights and hotel rooms. The outfits, the drinks and dining out.
By the time your voice is raw from scream-singing along with 50,000 fans in a packed stadium, you're down $2,000 — easily.

Attending a concert is no longer always just a night out. With the rise of music residencies and select-city tours, artists can save on travel costs while fans are shelling out for what's being sold as the trip of a lifetime.

While the residency was once synonymous with aging artists in Las Vegas, Celine Dion helped show its broader potential, staging blockbuster runs that revitalized her career and, more recently, launched her to a residency in Paris.

In the last year alone, Bad Bunny and Harry Styles have held runs of more than 30 shows in Puerto Rico and New York City, respectively. And in February, the Backstreet Boys will begin a 12-night run in Toronto that the group says will be its only North American live performances of the year.
The benefits for artists are compelling: residencies can eliminate travel, teardown and setup costs, reduce environmental impacts and limit the physical and psychological toll of touring.

But they can also make music less accessible, though some fans save for the experience as they would for a vacation, said Leonieke Bolderman, an assistant professor at the University of Groningen in the Netherlands who researches music tourism.
"Visiting concerts is becoming increasingly expensive, and indeed it will prohibit people from going," she said.

There's also a limit to what the market will support, she said, noting that some of the Harry Styles shows in Amsterdam this spring did not sell out — although nearly half a million people still reportedly attended.

Leonieke Bolderman, an assistant professor at the University of Groningen in the Netherlands who studies music tourism, said that although live music is becoming less accessible for some fans, others will save for months in order to recapture a moment in their youth or to be part of a new tradition. (Submitted by Leonieke Bolderman)
"But there are still people who find the experience so powerful and important and really save up for it."

Until about a decade ago, travelling for music often focused on nostalgia: pilgrimages to Graceland and Dollywood or to Liverpool, England, to experience the origin story of the Beatles, Bolderman said.

items: Backstreet Boys add multiple dates to planned Toronto concerts

blocks.text: "I'd read some papers saying, 'Oh, music tourism will disappear because these generations will die and then this phenomenon will disappear' — and we haven't seen that at all."

Streaming services have also shifted the economics for musicians. In the past, much of an artist's income came from recorded music, while touring was often a promotional vehicle to drive album sales, said Eric Alper, a Toronto-based music publicist.
Now, much of the money is in live shows.

Consider the Backstreet Boys. If they fill the Rogers Centre's 55,000 seats each night in Toronto, they could gross $124 million before costs, based on 2024 figures suggesting live concert tickets cost an average of $188.
LISTEN | The rise of the music residency:
Cost of Living26:45Are we too loyal to our loyalty programs?
Artists can then invest some of the money saved on transportation into creating a show that people will fly across the country — or the world — to see, Alper said.

"[Fans] want recreations of the video, they want the greatest light show they've ever seen, they want drones overhead making screenshots," he said. "They want an Instagram-able and TikTok-able moment so they can share on their own socials that they're at the show and you're not."
When nostalgia and FOMO collide

Camille Wenner saw her feeds fill this summer with images of friends at the Backstreet Boys in Las Vegas. It brought her back to Friday-night sleepovers, Teen Vogue covers and an 11-year-old version of herself belting out I Want it That Way.
In August, she got to relive that feeling with her girlfriends at the Sphere as she watched her childhood crush, Nick Carter, and his bandmates perform.

"We spent a month all summer watching on Instagram as all of our girlfriends went weekend after weekend: friends from Vancouver, friends from Toronto," she told The Cost of Living. "It just created this hype — we couldn't wait to go."

The experience cost more than $1,000 for the ticket and her share of four nights at the hotel. While she initially scored a reasonably priced flight, she said the trip ultimately cost more than $1,500 after it was affected by the WestJet flight attendant strike in August.
She was paying for the memories, she said — not just those from her preteen years, but also the chance to make new ones with friends.
"You can't do the trip on a budget," she said.
What it means for smaller artists and smaller cities
Bad Bunny's Puerto Rico residency injected an estimated $200 million US into the local economy, as fans flocked to San Juan where limited shows opened to people from outside Puerto Rico.
But most residencies take place in easier-to-reach destinations that already have the infrastructure needed to support an influx of thousands of tourists.

That's why Las Vegas, Toronto, Nashville, Paris, New York, Berlin and London have been home to these megaconcerts in recent years, said Bolderman. For the shows to succeed, there needs to be easy airport access, enough hotel rooms, a strong public transit system and, often, other attractions.

Puerto Rican rapper Bad Bunny performs live on stage as part of his two-day concert in San Juan, Puerto Rico in December 2021. This summer, he had a 31-concert residency in the U.S. territory. (Ricardo Arduengo/AFP via Getty Images)
Smaller cities, meanwhile, are less likely to be selected.

But that can present a different opportunity, Bolderman said, noting research suggesting smaller cities can play a role in supporting up-and-coming artists. In Ottawa, for example, the city hired Mathieu Grondin in 2024 as its first nightlife commissioner.
"For the cities that don't have the big headliners anymore, they can invest in a smaller music scene," she said. "And that can be more affordable for local people, local fans."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Laura Fraser is a senior writer and editor with CBC Radio and is based in Halifax. She writes about justice, health and the human experience. Story ideas are welcome at laura.fraser@cbc.ca

articles.title: Roles for trans and non-binary characters are vanishing, actors and experts warn
articles.summary: The recent success of high-profile 2SLGBTQ+ shows like Heated Rivalry may make it seem like Canada is providing a wealth of queer representation, but actors and experts tell CBC that complex trans…

image.caption: As anti-trans rhetoric drives increasing repression of trans and non-binary rights, it's also making big studios pull back on commitments to diversity in film and TV, experts say. Actors like Asher Rose and advocates say this makes it harder to combat 2SLGBTQ+ hate, which is more crucial than ever.

blocks.text: Last week, actor Asia Kate Dillon shared that nearly a decade after breaking boundaries playing the first non-binary main character in a major North American TV show, they are seeking a job in the service industry amid diminishing opportunities for trans performers.

The post from Dillon, who played Taylor Mason on the Showtime drama Billions from 2017 to 2023, comes a month after non-binary actor Jack Haven, known for Atypical and I Saw the TV Glow, made a plea on social media for casting roles to earn $4,000 US to qualify for SAG-AFTRA health insurance.
And despite a standout performance in Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey, Canadian actor Elliot Page said earlier this year he hasn't been getting casting calls.
It's part of a trend that actors and experts tell CBC News we're seeing in Canada as well.

While hit shows like Crave's Heated Rivalry, which features many cisgender queer characters and a trans actor in a small role, have made strides for 2SLGBTQ+ representation, complex trans stories are increasingly disappearing from screens amid rising anti-trans rhetoric across the globe. Experts warn this only makes it harder to combat dehumanizing myths.

"I can count on one hand the number of auditions I've had this year for film and TV work," Asher Rose, a non-binary actor and chair of the gender diversity subcommittee at ACTRA Toronto, told CBC News.

Asia Kate Dillon, left, seen here attending MGM+'s New York premiere of A Spy Among Friends in 2023, and Jack Haven, right, seen at the New York premiere of Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma in August 2026, have both recently made social media posts referencing difficulties in finding roles. (Jamie McCarthy/Getty Images and CJ Rivera/Invision/The Associated Press)

Streamers and big networks are caving to the cultural creep of conservatism, Rose said, and "consider trans stories, trans actors and trans characters to be too specific, potentially too alienating, as opposed to just part of human experience."
Actor Izaiah Dockery told CBC News he used to get multiple auditions a week, but now the few he gets as a Black trans man are smaller and more likely to rely on racial stereotypes.
When he tried to pitch a series he co-wrote that had a mainly trans cast, "the feedback we kept getting from broadcasters was that it was too in-your-face."
Izaiah Dockery says the number of auditions he's being offered has gone down sharply in recent years, and those that he does get often rely on stereotypes. (Izaiah Dockery)
Trans representation in film vanishing: GLAAD
When GLAAD started tracking representation in film in 2013, 14 films contained at least one 2SLGBTQ+ character.
Representation climbed through the 2010s, but after peaking in the early 2020s, it’s on the decline again, according to GLAAD's latest Where We Are in Film report, released this July.
It's worse for trans characters. In 2022, there were 12 films judged as transgender-inclusive by GLAAD. This dropped to two films in 2023 and 2024 and zero in 2025.
Of the 225 films released by Top 10 distributors in 2025, seven included a non-binary character and zero included a trans character.

"I feel like we've done a kind of 360 in the last 12 years, where there was very little representation of trans people and then we grew to a more encouraging place ... [and now] we've gone back to the start of that circle, only worse, actually," said writer and director Shelley Thompson, who directed the film Dawn, Her Dad & the Tractor.
The film, about a trans woman returning home to her town in Nova Scotia, was released in 2022, at a time when trans representation on screen seemed to be hitting its stride.

A still from Dawn, her Dad & the Tractor. The film revolves around a young transgender woman who returns to her family farm for the first time since her transition. (Dawn, her Dad & the Tractor/New Dawn Films)
But Thompson says it would be harder to make and distribute that film today. She says big industry players see diversity as a trend, not a natural part of life and art.
"And the trend of the trans storyline, I think that's underwater at the moment."
'Cancel Your Gays'
Although there's more representation in television than film, it's precarious, according to GLAAD.

While 2SLGBTQ+ characters on TV screens had gone up as of May 2025, GLAAD found, around 41 per cent were slated to disappear due to series ending, being cancelled, limited series formats or a character dying or leaving the show. This jumped to 61 per cent for trans characters. Only four trans characters appeared on series that had been officially renewed, GLAAD's data shows.
Fans dubbed it "Cancel Your Gays" in 2024 after the trend was identified, playing on the "Bury Your Gays" trope of the 2010s, where queer characters were often swiftly killed off.
Many shows featuring trans and non-binary characters, such as Heartstopper, Umbrella Academy, 911: Lone Star and Star Trek: Discovery, ended or were cancelled in the last two years.

items: 'Cancel Your Gays' trend sees 2SLGBTQ+ characters disappearing from TV

blocks.text: Shows like HBO Max’s cult hit Our Flag Means Death — cancelled in 2024 — can have a massive impact for queer audiences, Rose said.
A still from feature film Violence (2025), directed by Connor Marsden, showing actors Asher Rose and Rohan Campbell. (Violence)

Seeing characters like pirate Jim Jimenez, played by the non-binary actor Vico Ortiz, and Rhys Darby's Stede, who falls in love with a man late in life, helped Rose see they could discover their true self at any age.
"For this silly, wonderful comedy, it was kind of life-changing in a lot of ways."
Although a few new shows offer that representation, such as Crave's sapphic softball show Slo Pitch, co-produced by Page, the numbers don't replace what's been cancelled.

Fewer TV shows are being produced overall, according to industry data tracker Luminate, but this doesn't explain the sharp decline in 2SLGBTQ+ characters, Madelaine Rose, chair of the Progress Pride Committee at ACTRA National, told CBC News.
"Why are the queer ones the first [characters] being cut?" she said.
Our Flag Means Death, the cult hit from HBO Max, was one of many ground-breaking shows centering 2SLGBTQ+ storylines that was cancelled in 2024. (HBO Max/Crave)
Anti-trans rhetoric spreading
Experts say it's connected to the surge in anti-2SLGBTQ+ and anti-trans rhetoric in recent years in the U.S. and Canada.

A spokesperson for the U.S. Pentagon called the hit 2025 Netflix series Boots, about a gay Marine in the 1990s, "woke garbage" last October. Boots was cancelled by December, despite its first season outperforming Netflix titles that were renewed, according to Netflix data. Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos told Variety it was a business decision and was "absolutely not" connected to political backlash.

U.S. states have passed hundreds of bills since 2021 restricting trans people's access to health care, revoking their legal IDs and barring them from sports teams and public bathrooms that align with their gender.

items: Trump claims there are only '2 genders.' Historians say that's never been true

blocks.text: Trans rights teeter 'on a knife's edge' as U.S. midterms near
Several Canadian provinces, including Saskatchewan, Quebec and Alberta, have adopted anti-trans policies in recent years, including a ban on gender-affirming care for trans youth in Alberta.

We're seeing a "well-orchestrated effort to challenge human rights and inclusion in public life," driven by anti-trans misinformation, said Andrew Perez, executive director at 2SLGBTQ+ advocacy group Egale Canada.

items: New regulations on flags flown at Alberta schools to take effect in January
2SLGBTQ+ community worries about Trump's anti-trans rhetoric coming to Canada

blocks.text: That stretches to inclusion on the screen, he said.

The success of Heated Rivalry, the most-watched original series in Crave's history, demonstrates the demand is there for 2SLGBTQ+ storylines, Perez said, but "creative industries, the film industry, the theatre industry, don't exist in a vacuum and can become more cautious when facing political pressure or perceived controversy."
Alberta trans rights advocates take federal inquiry call to Parliament Hill
Between 2020 and 2024, police-reported hate crimes targeting gender identity or expression in Canada nearly tripled.

items: Statistics Canada numbers show Canadians becoming less accepting of gender diversity
Calgary students stage widespread school walkout to protest Alberta's transgender laws

blocks.text: Jo Vannicola, an Emmy award-winning Canadian actor and author, says Canada is growing less safe for trans and non-binary people, sharing they've experienced harassment in public as recently as two weeks ago.

It's a result of the snowball effect of less representation, they said: when there are fewer well-rounded trans characters onscreen, there are fewer counter-narratives to hateful misinformation put out by anti-trans politicians.
Jo Vannicola says Canada is growing less safe for trans and non-binary people, sharing that they've experienced hateful attacks as recently as two weeks ago. (Jo Vannicola)

"It … removes the ability for people in the heterosexual, cisgender world to really learn about who we are. And we do everybody a disservice by not doing that. We keep people divided and we keep hate alive."

As opportunities vanish, the community is making its own. This week, Vannicola launched the Queer & Trans Legacy Initiative, aimed at providing more opportunities for trans performers and works, with a live reading of a new screenplay, They, in Toronto.
Actors perform the screenplay They at a reading at Buddies in Bad Times Theatre in Toronto on Wednesday during the launch of the Queer & Trans Legacy Initiative. (Jo Vannicola)
But without mainstream backing, they won't be able to reach as many eyes.
"You're not going to erase us," Vannicola said. "So let us live, let us make work, let us contribute to the culture and contribute back to us because we deserve it."

articles.title: Young men and right-leaning podcasters helped Trump win in 2024. Both have soured on him
articles.summary: Young men are increasingly turned off by U.S. President Donald Trump, and right-leaning podcasters are distancing themselves, too — a trend that experts say could swing House and potential Senate…

image.caption: Supporters try to get a view of then-Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump as he arrives at a campaign rally at Albuquerque International Sunport on Oct. 31, 2024, in Albuquerque, N.M. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Like many young men, Nicholas Aparicio's concerns about future employment, buying a home or even putting gas in his car are mounting.
"The idea of starting a family feels very out of reach these days," the 20-year-old told CBC News.
Aparicio, a political science student in Binghamton, N.Y., says he voted for Donald Trump in 2024 because he believed the president would improve the economy and his own prospects.

"The fact that he was so personable and he was this entertainer, it felt good to have him in your corner. Like, that's my guy. He's not like us, because he's a billionaire, but he's willing to empathize with us," Aparicio said. "He's going to fight for us."
Aparicio's attitude now: "I feel like we got duped."
While Aparicio is the president of the College of Republicans Binghamton Chapter, he's so disillusioned with the party that he’s not sure he will even vote in next week’s midterms.

Nick Aparicio, a political science student living in Binghamton, N.Y., voted for Donald Trump in 2024 because he believed the president would improve the economy and his own prospects. Aparicio thinks differently now. (Yanjun Li/CBC)

For years, it felt like many young men were all in on President Trump and his Make America Great Again platform. So were many popular right-leaning or "manosphere" podcasters, like Joe Rogan and Tucker Carlson, who helped spread Trump’s message in the run-up to the 2024 election.
Together, these groups helped get him re-elected.
But young men are increasingly turned off by Trump, and those podcasters are distancing themselves, too — a trend that experts say could swing House and potential Senate seats in the midterms.
"At this point, Democrats have a 26-point lead on Republicans amongst younger people," said John Della Volpe, director of polling at the Harvard Institute.
Midterms outcome rests largely on young men
Della Volpe’s recent poll found just nine per cent of young Americans believe the country is on the right track, while 69 per cent say they're fearful about the future.
The same poll found only 31 per cent of young men said they would definitely vote.
"Young men absolutely helped Trump win in the last election and if they don’t come out and vote in these midterms, it will change the outcome."
David Sasaki, a director at the American Institute for Boys and Men, says that many Gen Z men are avid listeners of podcasters like Rogan, Steven Bartlett and standup comedian Andrew Schulz.

"I think that [young men] feel that they are being spoken to, not just about. It's using language that they use, it's using cultural references and jokes they understand, it’s very relatable," Sasaki said.
Cross Country Checkup is asking: How will the U.S. midterm elections affect you? What questions do you have? Leave your comment here and we may read it or call you back for this Sunday's show.
He said that "authenticity, or at least perceived authenticity, is the currency of politics these days." He also said that podcasters fill a void in some young men.

"A lot of [them] are not growing up with mentors, role models or male adults in their real life, and they’re finding them online," Sasaki said. "They have a lot of influence over these voters, who matter a lot come election day."
Young men and right-leaning podcasters
Aparicio says while he doesn’t listen to one particular podcaster, like many of his peers, he consumes their content through social media clips.

In 2024, Rogan, Schulz and Theo Von all hosted Donald Trump on their shows and spoke about MAGA politics — which is, generally speaking, anti-establishment, anti-immigrant and anti-foreign entanglements — in a way that seemed to endorse it.
But that's changing.

Last year, Schulz said on his podcast Flagrant that he regretted voting for Trump. In April, Carlson, the former Fox News personality and now host of the podcast The Tucker Carlson Show, also expressed regret at endorsing Trump in 2024, saying "I’m sorry for misleading people" and that he will be "tormented" by it.
Meanwhile, Rogan — still the most popular podcaster in the U.S. — has publicly criticized Trump twice: over the White House hosting a UFC fight this summer and the war in Iran.

Comedian and podcaster Theo Von, in glasses, arrives prior to the second inauguration of President Donald Trump at the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 20, 2025. Since then, Von has been more critical of the president. (Al Drago-Pool/Getty Images)
CBC reached out to Rogan, Von, Schulz and Carlson for comment but did not hear back in time for publication.
Right-leaning podcasters mentioning Trump less

In an effort to quantify conservative podcasters' disenchantment with Trump, The Wall Street Journal studied how often podcasters such as Rogan and Ben Shapiro have referred to him since the lead-up to the 2024 presidential election. According to the Journal’s reporting, mentions of Trump have dropped 70 per cent.

"There were two main plunges: one was right after the election, after which it steadily dropped, and then it dipped again after the Iran war started," Wall Street Journal reporter Neil Mehta told CBC News.
Wall Street Journal reporter Neil Mehta has studied how right-leaning podcasters have covered Donald Trump since he was elected president a second time. (CBC)
"Podcasters and content creators are the predominant source of news for young people. But they also prioritize being seen as real and authentic — that’s the sell," Mehta said.
For Sasaki, a number of pivotal moments demonstrate the podcasters' shift away from Trump.
In early October, Theo Von, who hosts This Past Weekend, interviewed New York's left-leaning Mayor Zohran Mamdani. They discussed socialism, affordability and inequality.

"This to me showed what we already could see … that the conversation was really changing," said Sasaki. "In the lead-up to the 2024 election, [Von] had Trump on, who appeared very relatable. And then Mamdani went on the show and appeared even more relatable."
Sasaki also pointed to CBS News exit polling data that showed roughly 60,000 Americans who voted for Trump in 2024 also voted for Mamdani in 2025.

"What Trump and that campaign was able to do in 2024 was go to the spaces where young men were, speak to them in their vernacular with cultural references that they relate to, and say, ‘I know that you’re struggling, I see your struggles and we’re going to do something about it,’" Sasaki said.
But "assuming this demographic of young men is all in on MAGA and can’t swing [away] would be an error in judgment."
Trump out of step with young men: expert
Aparicio said that by potentially not voting in this year's midterms, "I want to emphasize the point that young men should not be taken for granted by the Republicans."
Podcaster Joe Rogan has publicly criticized Donald Trump twice this year, including calling the war in Iran a 'giant quagmire' and not what his MAGA followers voted for. (The Joe Rogan Show/YouTube)
Ultimately, Sasaki believes Trump may be missing what young men in 2026 really care about.
"This demographic is more worried than ever about the economy. They feel very little job security, many can’t imagine ever buying a home and are even living below the poverty line," he said.
Aparicio says Trump began looking untrustworthy shortly after he won in 2024.
"The first real sign was him campaigning that he would release the Epstein files and then began gaslighting his followers [when he took office] and saying they don't exist," he said.
He also believes the economy has gotten worse and that the U.S. involvement in the war in Iran and its endorsement of Israel's actions in Gaza are making things harder for Americans.
"Hopefully if I work hard, I will be able to afford a home and raise a family," Aparicio said.
"The way things are going, I really don’t feel sure about that."

articles.title: Prince Harry says he wants to reconcile with the Royal Family. It may not be so easy
articles.summary: As much as Prince Harry may signal his desire to reconcile with the Royal Family, making it happen could be a challenge.

image.caption: After several years of estrangement from other members of the Royal Family, Prince Harry says he would like to reconcile. (Aaron Chown/Reuters)

blocks.text: As far as open appeals go, it couldn’t be much clearer: Prince Harry wants a rapprochement with the Royal Family.
After several years of estrangement — particularly from elder brother Prince William — the Duke of Sussex has taken to sending public signals of a desire to overcome the discord.
The most recent came in an interview with GQ magazine, where he was asked about the "complicated relationship" he has with William and their father, King Charles.
"With everything else that's going on in the world, the most important thing is to reconcile. That's the key point," Harry said.
As much as Harry may signal the desire to reconcile, making it happen could be a challenge.

"I think on a personal level, King Charles III will want to spend time with his grandchildren, so I can see a personal reconciliation happening on that level," Toronto-based royal author and historian Carolyn Harris said in an interview.
Harry arrives to visit the Community Recording Studio in Nottingham, central England, on Oct. 15. (Joe Giddens/AFP/Getty Images)
"In the wider Royal Family, it seems very unlikely that a reconciliation will take place, because of all the events that have unfolded over the past six years."
Harry and his wife, Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, stepped back as working members of the Royal Family in 2020 and moved to California.

During their time in the U.S., a Netflix docuseries, an interview with Oprah Winfrey and Harry's memoir Spare offered a panoply of their views, including pointed criticism of the Royal Family. Harry and Meghan returned to the U.K. with their two children in August.

items: Prince Harry told his story in his own words. But what happens now?
What we learned from Netflix's docuseries about Prince Harry and Meghan Markle

blocks.text: Buckingham Palace and the King have made it clear they remain non-working royals, but Harry and Meghan have been at public engagements that for the average passerby would look very similar to regular royal events.

"You're hearing things like what was in the Sunday Times the other week that they don't like the term 'working royal' and that they consider themselves to be royals who work," said Craig Prescott, a constitutional expert and lecturer in law at Royal Holloway.

"So it's all … quite confusing in some way, because if you wanted to seek reconciliation with the broader Royal Family, don't let it come out that you don't like the term that defines them rather than you."
Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, centre, and Harry, right, visit Himmah Hub, a food poverty charity, during their time in Nottingham, England, on Oct. 15. (Annabel Lee-Ellis/Getty Images)
Making the latest overture in public could also have an impact on its effectiveness.

"The more that Prince Harry speaks to the press, the less likely it is that a reconciliation … will take place, as there are likely concerns among his wider family that if they do meet with Prince Harry, he will speak of it in future interviews," Harris said.
In a way, Prescott suggested, Harry and Meghan are trying to achieve private things by going public.
"Generally, that's not how the monarchy works."
"The monarchy has always tried to keep a … distinction [between the private and public roles], and William, I think, is very keen on that distinction," Prescott said.
William, Prescott noted, "talks about going to work."
"And so the whole way Harry has gone about this is almost an anathema to how William wants to do this."

Harry, left, Prince William, centre, their father the then-Prince of Wales Charles, and David Attenborough attend the global premiere for Our Planet at the Natural History Museum in London on April 4, 2019. (John Sibley/Getty Images)
Rifts among royals are nothing new. Sometimes, rapprochement has indeed followed.
"During the medieval period, there was a kind of formal ceremony of reconciliation," said Harris.
"There were so many conflicts between royal fathers and sons, royal brothers, that there would be a big show of forgiveness … often facilitated by royal women who were seen as peacemakers."
More recently, one of the more notable rifts came between King Edward VIII and the Royal Family after his abdication in 1936.
"He was very much out and stayed out for the rest of his life," said Prescott.
Of course, there are differences, given that Edward was a former King.

King Edward VIII, left, followed by Albert, the Duke of York, during a visit to Scotland in 1936. Edward abdicated on Dec. 10, 1936. He was succeeded by the duke, who became King George VI. (Fox Photos/Hulton Archive/Getty Images)

"You had a very young Queen [Elizabeth] and you had a middle-aged [former] King, and there was always perhaps a concern in the early days of there being a rival court that never really materialized," said Prescott.
"But with Harry, it's of course a little bit different. He's only the son of the King, not a former King. But you can still see that, in a sense, if you're in, you're in, if you're out, you're out."

Harry's situation has also spawned its own rarity in the royal annals, one that comes with its own bit of irony — it appears to have bolstered the relationship between two other members of the family.
The conflict with Harry has brought William and the King closer together, Harris said.

"Prince Harry's admitted royal history is not something he's particularly interested in," she said, "but when we do look at the sweep of royal history, it's rare for a monarch and an adult heir to be on the same page in this manner."
An acknowledgment of 'suffering' but no apology — yet
Charles, centre, joins a Junkanoo parade in Parliament Square in Nassau on Wednesday during his visit to the Bahamas. (Ben Stansall/Getty Images)

As the King set off for his Caribbean visit this past week, much attention focused on how he would address the devastating impacts of the transatlantic slave trade and calls for an apology and reparations from the British government.
On his first stop in the Bahamas, he acknowledged "the great suffering and injustices of the past in these islands and beyond."
Buckingham Palace called the first stop of his three-country visit a "diplomatic success," but others felt Charles didn't go far enough.

"Acknowledgement is like when somebody hits your car and says, 'Oh, I'm sorry.' But the apology is when they hit your car, and say, 'I am sorry, and here's my insurance.' It's the difference between recognizing that something bad has happened and holding yourself accountable for it," Niambi Hall Campbell-Dean, chair of the Bahamas National Reparations Committee, told As It Happens host Nil Köksal.
"We need accountability. We don't just need statements of regret. Because we know that slavery was a bad thing. Everybody knows that slavery is a bad thing."

King Charles, right, walks on a wooden boardwalk through the mangrove ecosystem at Bonefish Pond National Park in New Providence, during his visit to the Bahamas on Wednesday. (Isabel Infantes/AFP/Getty Images)

Anything Charles says as the visit continues, particularly at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting [CHOGM] in Antigua and Barbuda this coming week, will be under continued scrutiny, especially in light of a shift in the British government's position on the issue on Friday.

Writing in The Guardian newspaper, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he is open to calls for a formal apology for Britain's historical role in slavery. He rejected calls for financial reparations, but said he wanted to "launch a new drive on debt," including by helping more vulnerable countries "repay over a longer time period and with better ⁠rates."
Burnham's statement "is clearly a big development," Prescott said, "and signifies a clear softening in the U.K. government’s stance."
For Charles, Prescott said, this "very much takes the heat off him."

"Up to now, the calls had been on the King to make an apology, which he would not do however loud those demands became, because ... it's not the government's position and ... of the possibility of opening the door to financial reparations."

items: King Charles acknowledges 'painful' past amid calls for Commonwealth discussions on reparations
King Charles's predecessors abetted the slave trade, and research aims to show what they knew

blocks.text: Burnham's statement has, Prescott said, shown there is room for some movement — he's opened the door to an apology, but ultimately on the condition that calls for financial reparations are dropped and the focus shifts to other avenues, such as debt forbearance or extending repayments.
"He has opened the door for political discussion and so that takes the focus away from the King to the politicians to potentially reach an agreement," he said.
"This is likely to dominate the CHOGM, and the King will refer to this, and perhaps support those efforts to reach an agreement, but the focus is taken away from him."
In the Bahamas, Charles appeared to receive a warm welcome, and garnered headlines for dancing in a street parade.

"King Charles has been well-received in the Bahamas and in Guyana and has shown a strong interest in engaging with both public figures at official events and the enthusiastic crowds who have gathered to greet him," Harris said.
"The King clearly enjoyed joining in the festivities in the Bahamas."
Charles, right, speaks with a local artisan who makes baskets in Parliament Square in Nassau on Wednesday. (Ben Stansall/AFP/Getty Images)
He also met with local boxers, and as is usual for his visits, spent some time focusing on local environmental issues.

From the Bahamas, Charles travelled to Guyana, where on Friday he undertook numerous engagements, including a visit to the Commonwealth War Graves. He also visited Independence Park, which marks the place where public executions occurred after the Demerara Slave Rebellion of 1823.

King Charles, second from left, visits Independence Park, which marks the site of public executions following the 1823 Demerara Slave Rebellion, in Georgetown, Guyana, on Friday. (Isabel Infantes/Getty Images)

He attended a biodiversity conference, met Indigenous leaders, attended a business reception and visited the Kingston Seawall. At the beach, he heard about efforts to restore mangrove ecosystems along the coastline.
Charles arrived in Antigua and Barbuda on Friday night, and will deliver the opening address at CHOGM on Tuesday.
A talk show and a tenant controversy

Prince William visits Lower Blakemere Farm, a Duchy Focus Farm, in Hereford, England, earlier this year. Plans by William's Duchy of Cornwall to sell land to raise money for other projects, including ones that focus on homelessness and climate change, have sparked controversy in Devon, in southern England. (Jacob King/Getty Images)

The headlines focused on Prince William in the past few days were a study in contrast, from the rousing welcome he received for a talk show appearance to controversy swirling around his Duchy of Cornwall's plans to sell land, leaving tenant farmers feeling betrayed.

"Once Harry and Meghan returned to the United Kingdom, there was speculation that the headlines would be all about Harry and Meghan, but as heir to the throne, Prince William is attracting headlines as well," Harris said.

William’s appearance on The Graham Norton Show came as a surprise to the audience as he promoted his Earthshot Prize environmental initiative. While on Norton's red couch, he offered up some chat show banter, with mentions of everything from his family's love of the TV show The Celebrity Traitors to how as a child he thought it was "quite cool" to be a police officer.
"He showed himself to be really relaxed," Prescott said, although he noted that he's not the first royal to do a talk show, with Princess Anne going on with BBC host Terry Wogan in the 1980s.
"It's not unheard of, but it is more unusual today."

The Duchy story struck a markedly different tone, with the headline in the Observer being: "'Charles was fantastic. William can go to hell': Duchy tenants face eviction as prince sells historic land."
That report focused on plans by the Duchy of Cornwall to sell land to raise money for other projects, including ones that focus on homelessness and climate change, two priorities for William.

"There has been some controversy surrounding his determination to sell off parts of the Duchy of Cornwall," said Harris, "as a sale of this kind can only be done once, and the Duchy of Cornwall was intended by King Edward III to provide an income for the heir to the throne. So the question arises: What if Prince George, when he comes of age, has different views?"

Prince William, left, meets Harry Davies, centre, the incoming tenant of the Duchy of Cornwall's first regenerative Farm Business Tenancy, during a visit to examine the role of regenerative farming in climate resilience on Oct. 1 in Hereford, England. The Prince of Wales visited to region to meet with those tackling the threat of flooding caused by extreme weather conditions. (Mathieu Willcocks/Getty Images)
Prescott said the land sale situation is a difficult one, particularly given the nature of the relationship between landlords and tenants.
"The landlord has the power and the tenant doesn't," he said.
"Intuitively, your sympathies are with the farmers, but this is where it just rubs up against the law and someone being a landlord."
Royally quotable
"Hearts, far from this valley, will ache with yours. Tears, from those who remember and those who at the time were not yet born, will be shed with yours."

— King Charles, in a speech to mark the 60th anniversary of the Aberfan disaster, when slurry from a collapsed colliery spoil tip slid down a mountain slope and engulfed a school and houses in the Welsh mining village of Aberfan, killing 116 children and 26 adults.

Queen Camilla, third from left, lays flowers at Aberfan Memorial Garden as King Charles, second from left, and Mair Morgan, left, the last surviving teacher from Pantglas Junior School, look on during a commemoration event to mark the 60th anniversary of the Aberfan disaster on Oct. 21 in Merthyr Tydfil, Wales. On Oct. 21, 1966, a mountain of liquefied coal waste slid into a valley, engulfing Pantglas Junior School and several surrounding houses. (Aaron Chown/Getty Images)
Royal reads

Detectives in Scotland are investigating Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell's stay at Balmoral castle as reported guests of Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor amid allegations that women were trafficked from the royal estate. [The Guardian]

Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, says she was "deeply distressed" by allegations that a collection of child sexual abuse images had been found at her father's former home. She also revealed that a letter containing "troubling allegations" about him had been sent to London police in 2018. The Metropolitan Police has since voluntarily referred itself to the police watchdog because it failed to pass on the letter to relevant overseas law enforcement agencies. [CBC, ITV]
The Royal Family welcomed the Sultan of Oman to Windsor for a state visit. [The Independent]
The Sultan of Oman, Haitham bin Tariq Al Said, left, speaks with King Charles, right, at a state banquet on Oct. 20 at Windsor Castle in Windsor, England. (Jordan Pettitt/Getty Images)
A teenager with a rare muscle disorder sang an Ed Sheeran song for the Princess of Wales during a visit to a children's hospice. [Ipswich Star]

When she was seven years old, Bayo Randle's great-great-grandmother Sarah Forbes Bonetta was presented to Queen Victoria at Windsor Castle as a "diplomatic gift" from an African king. Victoria would go on to pay for Bonetta's education, approve her marriage to one of west Africa's wealthiest men and become godmother to her eldest daughter. Now, as a biography is published, Randle has spoken of his family history. [The Guardian]
Catherine, Princess of Wales, centre, meets Charlotte Freegard, left, during a music therapy session at The Treehouse children's hospice in Ipswich, England, on Oct. 22. (Chris Radburn/Reuters)

articles.title: Canada shelves pledge to phase out captivity of elephants and great apes
articles.summary: The federal government has effectively shelved a bill meant to phase out the captivity and import and export of elephants and great apes in Canada. Some animal advocates suspect it has to do with the…

image.caption: Edmonton Valley Zoo attendant Paul Williams walks with Lucy the elephant in March 2023. Lucy was sold to the zoo in 1977 and has lived alone for much of the last two decades. A federal bill that sought to end new captivity of elephants and great apes has been shelved indefinitely. (Jason Franson/The

blocks.text: Canada·New

The federal government has effectively shelved a bill meant to phase out the captivity and import and export of elephants and great apes in Canada. Some animal advocates suspect it has to do with the government's current preoccupation with the tariff war and other economic issues.
Bill S-15, known as the Jane Goodall Act, died when Parliament was prorogued last January
A key piece of legislation aimed at phasing out elephant and great ape captivity in Canada has been shelved indefinitely.

After years of legislative progress and hurdles, the Jane Goodall Act, named after the renowned conservationist and primatologist, passed its third reading in the Senate in December 2024, but died when Parliament was prorogued in January 2025.

Despite various commitments made by the former Liberal government and a 2025 campaign pledge to reintroduce the act meant to protect captive elephants and great apes, there likely won't be a push by Ottawa to revive it anytime soon, say animal advocates who suspect it has to do with the government's current preoccupation with the tariff war and other economic issues.

The act was first introduced in 2020 by the late Manitoba Sen. Murray Sinclair, and later re-introduced by Sen. Marty Klyne. The act, which became known as Bill S-15, was also supported by Goodall, who died last year.

It sought to end new captivity, banning zoos and other establishments from importing and exporting great apes and elephants and breeding them, unless it was for the purpose of conservation, welfare or scientific research, rather than entertainment or commercial trade.

items: Trainer seriously injured after elephant attack at Ontario's African Lion Safari
Senators reject field trip to African Lion Safari amid elephant bill study

blocks.text: It would have also banned the use of the animals for entertainment, including elephant rides.
"Since the election occurred, we haven't seen any movement on this front," said Camille Labchuk, executive director of animal law advocacy organization Animal Justice.
Advocates, zoos urged government action

Almost a year after Prime Minister Mark Carney was elected, a group of animal advocates and zoos, including the Toronto and Calgary Zoos, sent a letter to current environment minister Julie Dabrusin in March, urging the government to "work to introduce and champion legislation to protect captive animals as soon as possible."
"We stand united in the belief that this federal law is not only necessary, but welcome," it stated.
However, the group did not get the response they hoped for.
In an email shared exclusively with CBC News, the group shared the minister's written response, which did not directly address the group's concern.

In part, the response read, "As you noted, Bill S-15 died on the Order Paper … in the previous session. The Government of Canada's broader legislative agenda is influenced by a range of factors, including decisions by the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons."
Johari, a nine-month-old baby western lowland gorilla rides on its mother Josephine's back at the Metro Toronto Zoo in February 2002. (Frank Gunn/The Canadian Press)

Dabrusin also highlighted other conservation initiatives Ottawa was championing. She said provinces and territories were primarily responsible for animal welfare, "including the regulation of zoos, and all have legislation in place addressing these matters. The Government of Canada will continue to monitor related developments."

Dabrusin was unavailable for an interview with CBC News. However, Keean Nembhard, a spokesperson for Dabrusin, said in a statement that "any future consideration of similar legislation would require it to be reintroduced, and at this time, no further decision has been made regarding the future of this bill."
He did not elaborate on why.
"It's incumbent on them to explain more to Canadians if they're backing away from this and why," said Labchuk.
She and other proponents of Bill S-15 point to various government pledges, including one made by former environment minister Steven Guilbeault when Goodall died last October.
Jane Goodall, conservationist & activist dies, aged 91
'Animals don't vote'
There are believed to be 23 elephants currently living in Canada, though the numbers are subject to some fluctuation.

There are three in Quebec at the Granby Zoo and one, Lucy, at the Edmonton Valley Zoo. One of the largest herds on the continent resides at African Lion Safari, near Hamilton. About 19 elephants are located at the Ontario park, though officials there would not confirm numbers to CBC News.
Environment and Climate Change Canada told CBC News two elephants were exported to the U.S. this year, though privacy laws would not allow it to disclose the exporter.

Angela Fernandez, director of the animal law program at the University of Toronto, who previously spoke in favour of the bill to legislators, calls the lack of action on the bill a "real lost opportunity."
She said so much work has been done already that it would be "low hanging fruit" for the government to "pick it up, dust it off and carry it over the finish line."

items: Elephant that attacked trainer still with herd at African Lion Safari
African Lion Safari ended elephant rides after 2019 attack. So why are they still allowed in Canada?
Texas zoo cancels controversial deal to buy African Lion Safari elephants for $2M

blocks.text: However, she says that may not happen any time soon.
"The Carney government is so focused on development and economic issues," she said. "It's a changed landscape."
Fernandez says, generally, animal legislation is tough to pass for a variety of reasons, including the feeling that "animals don't vote," which means laws protecting them may not be a priority.
With files from Carly Thomas

articles.title: After estimated $360 million in flood damage, why is province saying Niagara residents don't qualify for aid?
articles.summary: The devastating summer floods that hit north Niagara helped propel Canada's total insured damage from natural disasters over the summer to one of the worst on record, new data shows.

image.caption: St. Catharines riding MPP Jennie Stevens speaks at the Ontario legislature on Tuesday. She demanded the province activate the Disaster Recovery Assistance for Ontarians program for Niagara flooding victims. (Legislative Assembly of Ontario)

blocks.text: Hamilton
The devastating summer floods that hit north Niagara helped propel Canada's total insured damage from natural disasters over the summer to one of the worst on record, new data shows.
Flooding victims say feeling overwhelmed, devastated, anxious, helpless in survey

Those back-to-back storms overnight on July 27 and July 28 then again on Aug. 2 each dumped a month's worth of water in just a few hours, completely overwhelming the municipal sanitary sewer systems in St. Catharines, Lincoln, and parts of Niagara-on-the-Lake and Niagara Falls and leaving thousands of homes flooded.

Three months later, countless Niagara residents whose homes were flooded with sewage-tainted water remain in limbo as they try to get their insurance companies to settle what can be expensive claims, says St. Catharines riding MPP Jennie Stevens.
Many of those flooding victims say they feel overwhelmed, anxious, traumatized, helpless and even suicidal, a new survey of flooding victims has found.

Stevens stood up in the Ontario legislature this week and demanded the province activate a provincial disaster relief program to help Niagara people hammered by flooding, but ran into stiff resistance from Municipal Affairs and Housing Minister Rob Flack who said those flooded households don't qualify for that aid.
$360 million in flooding damage estimated

Toronto-based Catastrophe Indices and Quantification Inc. estimated the flooding in Niagara caused $360 million, a sizeable chunk of the estimated $3.7 billion in insured losses nation-wide over the summer that included severe storms across the prairies, wildfires in British Columbia and other natural disasters, the Insurance Bureau of Canada said on Oct. 22.
That was the third costliest summer in history for losses related to severe weather, the bureau said.

Earlier in the summer, Stevens wrote to Flack, asking him to consider making Niagara residents and businesses hit by flooding eligible for financial assistance under the Disaster Recovery Assistance for Ontarians (DRAO) program.

That program pays up to $250,000 to people, farmers, small businesses and not-for-profit agencies for emergency expenses, repairs and replacing essential property after natural disasters such as floods, tornadoes, landslides and earthquakes.

A provincial website says the disaster recovery program generally doesn't cover damage from sewer backups, except for a provision in which low-income households may qualify. But Stevens said in her letter to Flack that an Environment and Climate Change Canada meteorologist confirmed the July storm resulted in flash flooding.
The City of St. Catharines also said in a statement in the summer that the flooding was the result of a storm, not an infrastructure issue.

Ontario Municipal Affairs and Housing Minister Rob Flack speaks at the Ontario legislature on Tuesday after St. Catharines riding MPP Jenny Stevens demanded the province activate the Disaster Recovery Assistance for Ontarians program for Niagara flooding victims. (Legislative Assembly of Ontario)

Flack wasn't buying that when he responded to Stevens' demands during question period at Queen's Park on Tuesday that the province activate DRAO for the Niagara flooding victims. He said people with basements flooded by sewer backups need to go through private insurance.
"Bottom line is, DRAO was not activated because it was not overland water," he said. "It was sewer backups."
Stevens said the province has a duty to help Ontarians in times of disaster.
"[But] ninety two days later, still, no relief" in north Niagara, she said.

She noted an online group formed in the wake of the flooding, Northend Neighbours, did a survey of nearly 450 homeowners and found more than 60 per cent of those flooded "are still in limbo" with their insurance claims.
"Seniors and vulnerable families are drowning in repairs bills and fears of losing their homes," Stevens said.
Stop pointing fingers, Stevens said
"Stop pointing the finger and start taking responsibility. "The residents of St. Catharines cannot afford another day of delay."
Daya Lye, one of the organizers of the Northend Neighbours online survey, said only 36.6 per cent of respondents — 97 per cent of whom were flooded — have had their insurance claim fully approved.
Of those flooded, 70 per cent described the damage as severe or catastrophic, she said.

The flooding and the uncertainty over repairs has taken a huge psychological toll on residents as shown by their descriptions of their feelings in the survey, said Lye, who experienced minor flooding because she has a backflow valve at her home.
"They said overwhelmed, frustrated, stressed, depressed, PTSD, anxious, trauma, helpless, despair," she said. "People feel devastated. One person wrote 'suicidal'."
"That part was shocking to me how bad it was for people emotionally. It's definitely a mess."

Lye said some respondents said their insurance companies leapt into action almost right away, with an insurance adjuster calling within days of the flooding and remediation companies sent out almost immediately after that.
"There's a huge difference between people's insurance companies," she said.
The insurance bureau said claims from natural disasters continue to skyrocket in Canada.

Over the last decade, insured losses from extreme weather in Canada have averaged more than $3.7 billion annually, up from $1.4 billion in the previous decade and $883 million in the decade before that, its data shows. Annual losses have increased by roughly 300 per cent since the late 1990s and early 2000s, even after accounting for inflation, the bureau said.
The insurance bureau called on all levels of government to take immediate steps to reduce Canada's exposure to extreme weather events through steps such as:

items: Using land use planning to restrict development in areas at high risk of floods and wildfires.
Providing homeowners with incentives to invest in practical, affordable measures to reduce extreme weather damage.
Investing in resilient infrastructure to protect communities from extreme weather risks such as flooding.

blocks.text: ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Paul Forsyth is a St. Catharines-based CBC reporter covering communities in the Niagara Region. He has decades of reporting experience in Niagara, having worked for Niagara This Week, the St. Catharines Standard and the Welland Tribune before joining CBC. You can reach him at paul.forsyth@cbc.ca.
